# QuantCore-Labs

> Free, client-side quantitative finance micro-tools and a glossary of quant terms. Each tool is a single static page that computes in the browser; no sign-up, no data upload.

All tools document their formulas, units and conventions on-page. Glossary entries give a definition, formula, institutional usage and a tested Python reference implementation.

This file concatenates every Markdown page listed in https://quantcore-labs.com/llms.txt (tools, glossary terms and code snippets), separated by horizontal rules.

---

# Black-Scholes Option Greeks Calculator

> Client-side Black-Scholes-Merton pricer for European options with continuous dividend yield.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/option-greeks-calc/

## Inputs

- S: spot price (> 0)
- K: strike (> 0)
- T: days to expiry, converted as days / 365
- σ: annualised volatility, %
- r: continuously compounded risk-free rate, %
- q: continuous dividend yield, %
- r can be filled in one click from the U.S. Treasury par yield curve (published daily), interpolated to the option expiry and converted to continuous compounding

## Formulas

```
d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r − q + σ²/2)T] / (σ√T)
d2 = d1 − σ√T
C  = S e^(−qT) N(d1) − K e^(−rT) N(d2)
P  = K e^(−rT) N(−d2) − S e^(−qT) N(−d1)
Δc = e^(−qT) N(d1)          Δp = −e^(−qT) N(−d1)
Γ  = e^(−qT) φ(d1) / (S σ √T)
ν  = S e^(−qT) φ(d1) √T / 100
Θc = [−S e^(−qT) φ(d1) σ/(2√T) − rK e^(−rT) N(d2)  + qS e^(−qT) N(d1)]  / 365
Θp = [−S e^(−qT) φ(d1) σ/(2√T) + rK e^(−rT) N(−d2) − qS e^(−qT) N(−d1)] / 365
ρc = K T e^(−rT) N(d2) / 100   ρp = −K T e^(−rT) N(−d2) / 100
```

N(·): Hart (1968) double-precision rational approximation per West (2005), |error| < 1e−14.
At T = 0 or σ = 0 the tool returns the deterministic limit (discounted forward intrinsic; Γ = ν = 0).

## Units

- Vega: per 1 volatility point
- Theta: per calendar day (multiply by 365/252 for trading-day theta)
- Rho: per 1 percentage point in r

## Reference values (S=100, K=100, T=1y, σ=20%, r=5%, q=0)

| Metric | Call | Put |
|---|---|---|
| Price | 10.4506 | 5.5735 |
| Delta | 0.6368 | −0.3632 |
| Gamma | 0.01876 | 0.01876 |
| Vega | 0.3752 | 0.3752 |
| Theta/day | −0.01757 | −0.00454 |
| Rho | 0.5323 | −0.4189 |

## FAQ

- **Theta per day or year?** Per calendar day (annual / 365).
- **Vega scaling?** Price change per 1 vol point (dV/dσ / 100).
- **American or A-share ETF options?** BSM is European-only. Chinese exchange-listed ETF options (SSE 50 ETF, CSI 300 ETF) are European-style, so BSM is the reference model; American options with dividends need a tree or PDE solver.
- **CDF accuracy?** Hart/West, |error| < 1e−14.

## Limitations

- European exercise only; constant σ and r; no discrete dividends.
- Educational and analytical use only; not investment advice.

# Monte Carlo Asset Path Simulator

> Client-side Monte Carlo simulator of asset price paths under Geometric Brownian Motion (GBM), with terminal-price percentiles.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/tools/monte-carlo-asset-sim/

## Inputs

- Initial price S0
- Annual drift mu (%) and annual volatility sigma (%)
- Time horizon T (years) and time steps per year
- Number of simulated paths

## Model

```
dS_t = mu * S_t * dt + sigma * S_t * dW_t                      (GBM)
S_{t+dt} = S_t * exp( (mu - sigma^2/2) * dt + sigma * sqrt(dt) * Z ),  Z ~ N(0, 1)
```

The exact log-normal step is used, so there is no discretisation bias in the terminal distribution. Normal draws use the Box-Muller transform. Drift and volatility are constant, and increments are independent.

## Outputs

- Chart of the simulated paths
- Mean terminal price, plus the 5th, 50th and 95th percentiles of the terminal price S_T

## Notes

- The (mu - sigma^2/2) term comes from Ito's lemma. It makes E[S_T] = S0 * exp(mu * T) while the median is S0 * exp((mu - sigma^2/2) * T).
- The 5th percentile of S_T is a quantile of the price, not a VaR. Loss VaR is S0 minus that quantile, over the same horizon.
- Simulated paths can be used for path-dependent payoffs such as Asian, barrier or lookback options. Pricing them requires simulating under the risk-neutral drift (r - q) instead of mu.
- Educational and analytical use only; not investment advice.

---

# Markowitz Efficient Frontier Calculator

> Client-side mean-variance tool for three assets: plots random long-only portfolios in risk-return space and reports the highest-Sharpe portfolio found.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/tools/portfolio-efficient-frontier/

## Inputs

- Expected annual return and volatility for three assets (for example equities, bonds, alternatives)
- Risk-free rate R_f (%)
- Number of random portfolios to sample

## Method

```
R_p     = sum_i w_i * R_i
sigma_p = sqrt( w' * Sigma * w ),   Sigma_ij = sigma_i * sigma_j * rho_ij
Sharpe  = (R_p - R_f) / sigma_p
Weights: w_i >= 0, sum_i w_i = 1   (long-only, fully invested)
```

- The correlation between every pair of assets is fixed at rho = 0.3. It is not an input.
- Portfolios are generated by drawing three uniform numbers and normalising them to sum to 1. This samples the weight simplex non-uniformly: it concentrates around equal weights and under-samples corners.
- The reported "maximum Sharpe" portfolio is the best one among the sampled portfolios. It approximates the true tangency portfolio, and gets closer as the number of samples grows.

## Outputs

- Scatter of sampled portfolios (volatility vs expected return)
- Best-Sharpe portfolio: Sharpe ratio, expected return, volatility and weights

## Notes

- Diversification lowers risk whenever assets are less than perfectly correlated (rho < 1).
- Mean-variance results are very sensitive to expected-return inputs. Small changes can swing the weights.
- Educational and analytical use only; not investment advice.

---

# Performance & Drawdown Analytics Calculator

> Client-side calculator for Sharpe, Sortino, Calmar, CAGR, maximum drawdown, drawdown duration and VaR/CVaR from an equity curve, periodic returns or PnL.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/tools/performance-analytics/

## Inputs

- Data type: equity curve / NAV, periodic returns in % or decimal, or PnL per period plus starting capital
- One row per period; an optional leading date (YYYY-MM-DD, YYYY/MM/DD or YYYYMMDD) enables the monthly table and dated drawdown ranges
- Periods per year: 252 (US/global daily), 242 (A-share daily), 365, 52, 12
- Risk-free rate and Sortino MAR, % p.a. (MAR defaults to the risk-free rate)
- Risk-free rate can be filled in one click with the latest U.S. 3-month Treasury yield, converted to an effective annual rate

## Formulas

```
r_t     = E_t / E_(t-1) - 1          P = periods per year, n = number of returns
CAGR    = (E_n / E_0)^(P/n) - 1
Vol     = stdev(r, ddof=1) * sqrt(P)
rf_p    = (1 + rf)^(1/P) - 1
Sharpe  = mean(r - rf_p) / stdev(r - rf_p) * sqrt(P)
DD_down = sqrt(mean(min(r - MAR_p, 0)^2))      over all periods (Sortino-Price)
Sortino = (mean(r) - MAR_p) / DD_down * sqrt(P)
DD_t    = E_t / max(E_0..E_t) - 1,  MDD = min DD_t
Calmar  = CAGR / |MDD|                          full sample
VaR95   = -Q_5%(r),  CVaR95 = -mean(r | r <= Q_5%(r))   historical, linear interpolation
```

Skewness and excess kurtosis use population moment estimators. Drawdown duration counts periods from a peak until equity regains that peak; an unrecovered drawdown is counted to the last observation and flagged as ongoing.

## Outputs

Sharpe, Sortino, Calmar, CAGR, total return, annualised volatility, max drawdown with peak and trough dates, longest drawdown duration, current drawdown, best and worst period, VaR/CVaR 95%, win rate, profit factor, skewness, excess kurtosis. Charts: equity (linear or log), underwater, rolling Sharpe (63/126/252), with a synced crosshair readout, drag-to-zoom, 3M/6M/1Y/3Y range buttons and full statistics (return, CAGR, max DD, Sharpe, Sortino) for any selected period. Monthly returns table when dates are present.

## Reference check

Returns 1%, -2%, 3%, -1%, 2% with P = 252 and rf = 0: Sharpe 4.5932, Sortino 9.5247, MDD -2.00%, CAGR 332.56%, Calmar 166.28. Metrics are cross-checked against an independent NumPy/SciPy implementation, with relative difference below 1e-14.

## FAQ

- **252 or 242 days for A-shares?** 242 matches the A-share trading calendar; it changes Sharpe by about 2% versus 252.
- **Why does Sortino differ from other tools?** Some tools use the stdev of negative returns only; this one uses the full-sample downside deviation (Sortino-Price).
- **Calmar window?** Full sample, not the traditional trailing 36 months.
- **Is data uploaded?** No; all computation runs in the browser.

## Limitations

- Assumes equally spaced periods; irregular dates are not time-weighted.
- Historical VaR/CVaR are unreliable for short samples (fewer than ~250 observations).
- Educational and analytical use only; not investment advice.

# Implied Volatility Smile & Skew Calculator

> Client-side implied volatility solver and smile plotter for European options across strikes and expiries.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/tools/iv-smile/

## Input

- Rows of `days,strike,call,put` (comma, tab or semicolon). Either price may be blank or `-`.
- Spot S, rate r and dividend yield q in % p.a. These are used only when the forward cannot be inferred from put-call parity.
- Option: infer the forward from put-call parity (default on).
- For USD options, r can be filled in one click from the U.S. Treasury par yield curve at the median expiry (continuous compounding)

## Method

```
Black-76, D = e^(-rT), T = days/365
C = D [F N(d1) - K N(d2)],  P = D [K N(-d2) - F N(-d1)]
d1 = [ln(F/K) + s^2 T/2] / (s sqrt T),  d2 = d1 - s sqrt T

Forward from parity at K* = argmin |C - P|:  F = K* + (C - P)/D
Bounds: D max(F-K,0) < C < D F,   D max(K-F,0) < P < D K

Solver: Newton on s with vega; bracket [1e-6, 10] tightened by the sign of the error;
bisection whenever Newton leaves the bracket or vega < 1e-12; tol 1e-12

Smile per expiry: k = ln(K/F), OTM IV (puts K<F, calls K>=F)
IV(k) ~ a + b k + c k^2 (least squares): ATM IV = a, skew = b, curvature = c
```

## Output

- Call IV, put IV and OTM composite IV per strike; prices outside the bounds are flagged
- Per expiry: forward and its source, ATM IV, skew, curvature, number of valid points
- Charts: smile per expiry vs ln(K/F) or strike, with fitted curves; ATM IV term structure
- Volatility surface heatmap (log-moneyness x days). Each quoted expiry is a piecewise-linear OTM smile; between expiries, total variance w = IV^2 T is interpolated linearly in T at fixed ln(K/F), with no extrapolation
- Calendar-arbitrage check: reports any moneyness range where total variance falls from one expiry to the next
- Optional 3D surface view (Plotly gl3d, about 560 KB, loaded only when requested, with subresource integrity)

## Validation

- Round-trip over 466 grid cases covers T from 1 day to 3 years, K/F from 0.5 to 2, and sigma from 3% to 250%. All 466 converge, the price error is at most 1e-12, and no case needs more than 22 iterations.
- Against SciPy brentq on 300 random cases, the maximum IV difference is 7.6e-7. Both differences come from near-zero-vega cases, where the solver here is closer to the true sigma.
- A synthetic smile with a hidden 1% dividend yield is recovered exactly: forward, ATM IV, skew and curvature.

## FAQ

- **Why OTM options?** They are almost pure time value, so their IV is less sensitive to forward and quote errors.
- **Why not plain Newton?** Vega vanishes for deep ITM/OTM and short expiries; the safeguarded solver always converges inside the bounds.
- **China 50ETF/300ETF options?** European-style; use mid prices and parity-inferred forward.
- **Skew meaning?** dIV/dk at the money; -0.30 means about +3 vol points at a strike 10% below the forward.

## Limitations

- European exercise only; American options need a tree or PDE pricer.
- Uses a single discount rate per expiry; no bid/ask weighting in the fit.
- Educational and analytical use only; not investment advice.

---

# Volume-Weighted Average Price (VWAP)

> The ratio of cumulative traded value to cumulative volume over a horizon. The standard benchmark for judging institutional execution quality.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vwap/

Category: Execution & Market Microstructure. Term ID: `vwap`.

## Definition

VWAP is the average price of all trades over a period, with each trade weighted by its size. It equals total traded value divided by total traded volume.

## Formula

```
VWAP = Σᵢ pᵢ·vᵢ / Σᵢ vᵢ

pᵢ : price of trade i        (bar data: typical price (H + L + C) / 3)
vᵢ : volume of trade i
Σ  : over all trades in the horizon (usually one session, reset at the open)

Execution cost vs. VWAP (bps) = side × (P̄_fill − VWAP) / VWAP × 10⁴
side = +1 for buys, −1 for sells; positive = worse than benchmark
```

## Institutional usage

- **Execution benchmark.** Brokers and buy-side trading desks report slippage against interval VWAP. Beating VWAP on a buy means the average fill came in below it.
- **VWAP algorithms.** These split a parent order across the day in proportion to a forecast intraday volume profile, so the fills track the market's own VWAP. The main risk is a bad volume forecast.
- **Intraday signal.** Price relative to running VWAP is a common mean-reversion and trend filter. Anchored VWAP measures from a chosen event, such as earnings or a gap.

## Pitfalls

- Bar-based VWAP built from typical price only approximates trade-level VWAP. Use tick data when the result is used for cost attribution.
- Decide whether opening and closing auctions are included. On A-share markets the 09:15–09:25 call auction and the 14:57–15:00 closing auction can carry significant volume.
- A large order is part of the VWAP it is measured against. Participation above roughly 10–20% of volume makes the benchmark easy to "beat" and less informative; compare with arrival price as well.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy, pandas. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vwap/vwap.py

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def vwap(price: pd.Series, volume: pd.Series) -> float:
    """Session VWAP: sum(p * v) / sum(v)."""
    v = volume.astype(float)
    return float((price * v).sum() / v.sum())

def intraday_vwap(bars: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Series:
    """Running VWAP that resets each trading day.
    bars: DatetimeIndex, columns high, low, close, volume."""
    tp = (bars["high"] + bars["low"] + bars["close"]) / 3.0  # typical price
    pv = tp * bars["volume"]
    day = bars.index.normalize()
    return pv.groupby(day).cumsum() / bars["volume"].groupby(day).cumsum()

def slippage_bps(avg_fill: float, bench_vwap: float, side: int) -> float:
    """Execution cost vs VWAP in basis points. side=+1 buy, -1 sell.
    Positive = worse than VWAP."""
    return side * (avg_fill - bench_vwap) / bench_vwap * 1e4
```

## FAQ

**Is VWAP the same as TWAP?**

No. TWAP weights every time interval equally; VWAP weights by traded volume, so it follows the market's intraday volume curve.

## Related

- [Order Flow Imbalance (OFI)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/ofi/)
- [Amihud Illiquidity Measure (ILLIQ)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/amihud-illiquidity/)

# Order Flow Imbalance (OFI)

> Net buy-minus-sell pressure at the best bid and ask, measured from changes in top-of-book prices and sizes. Short-horizon price changes are approximately linear in OFI.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/ofi/

Category: HFT & Order Book Dynamics. Term ID: `ofi`.

## Definition

Order Flow Imbalance aggregates every event at the best quotes (limit orders, cancellations and market orders) into one signed number. Demand added at the bid or supply removed from the ask counts as positive; supply added at the ask or demand removed from the bid counts as negative.

## Formula

```
Per-event contribution (Cont, Kukanov & Stoikov, 2014):

eₙ =  1{Pᴮₙ ≥ Pᴮₙ₋₁}·qᴮₙ − 1{Pᴮₙ ≤ Pᴮₙ₋₁}·qᴮₙ₋₁
    − 1{Pᴬₙ ≤ Pᴬₙ₋₁}·qᴬₙ + 1{Pᴬₙ ≥ Pᴬₙ₋₁}·qᴬₙ₋₁

OFIₖ = Σ eₙ   over events n in interval k

Price impact:  ΔPₖ ≈ βₖ · OFIₖ + εₖ,   βₖ ∝ 1 / average depth

Pᴮ, qᴮ : best bid price and size     Pᴬ, qᴬ : best ask price and size
```

## Interpretation

- When the bid price is unchanged, the bid term reduces to the change in bid size. A rising bid counts the full new size, and a falling bid subtracts the full old size. The ask side mirrors this with the sign flipped.
- The original study on US equities reports that a single linear OFI regression explains a large share of short-interval mid-price variance. It also finds that the impact coefficient scales inversely with market depth.

## Institutional usage

- Short-horizon alpha and quote-skewing signals for market makers.
- Execution: pausing or accelerating child orders when OFI runs against the order.
- Multi-level OFI, computed over the top N levels, adds information beyond level 1 in deeper books.

## Pitfalls

- Snapshot data such as the 3-second L2 snapshots common in A-share feeds hides intermediate events, so OFI computed from snapshots is a coarse approximation.
- Normalise by average depth or volume before comparing OFI across stocks.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy, pandas. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/ofi/ofi.py

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def ofi(book: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Series:
    """Per-event order flow imbalance e_n (Cont, Kukanov & Stoikov, 2014).
    book: rows are successive top-of-book snapshots with columns
          bid_px, bid_sz, ask_px, ask_sz.
    Sum e_n over a time window to get OFI for that window."""
    bp, bq = book["bid_px"], book["bid_sz"]
    ap, aq = book["ask_px"], book["ask_sz"]
    bp0, bq0, ap0, aq0 = bp.shift(), bq.shift(), ap.shift(), aq.shift()
    e = (np.where(bp >= bp0, bq, 0.0) - np.where(bp <= bp0, bq0, 0.0)
         - np.where(ap <= ap0, aq, 0.0) + np.where(ap >= ap0, aq0, 0.0))
    e = pd.Series(e, index=book.index)
    e.iloc[0] = 0.0  # no previous snapshot
    return e

# Window OFI, e.g. 10-second buckets:
# ofi_10s = ofi(book).resample("10s").sum()
```

## FAQ

**Can OFI be computed from trade data alone?**

No. OFI needs best bid/ask prices and sizes. Trade-only data gives trade-sign imbalance (buy volume minus sell volume), a related but different measure.

## Related

- [Volume-Weighted Average Price (VWAP)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vwap/)
- [Hurst Exponent (H)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/hurst-exponent/)

# Hurst Exponent (H)

> A scaling exponent that measures long-range dependence in a time series. H < 0.5 indicates mean reversion, H = 0.5 a random walk, and H > 0.5 a persistent, trending series.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/hurst-exponent/

Category: Time Series & Stat-Arb. Term ID: `hurst-exponent`.

## Definition

The Hurst exponent H describes how the spread of a process grows with the time horizon. For a series with Hurst exponent H, the typical size of a move over τ steps scales as τᴴ. A random walk has H = 0.5.

## Formula

```
Rescaled range (R/S) on returns xₜ, window length n:
  Yₜ = Σ_{s≤t} (xₛ − x̄)            cumulative deviation
  R(n) = max Yₜ − min Yₜ ,  S(n) = std(x)
  E[R(n)/S(n)] ∝ nᴴ   →  H = slope of log(R/S) vs log n

Lagged-difference scaling on log prices pₜ:
  std(pₜ₊τ − pₜ) ∝ τᴴ   →  H = slope of log std vs log τ

H < 0.5 anti-persistent (mean-reverting)
H = 0.5 uncorrelated increments (random walk)
H > 0.5 persistent (trending)
```

## Institutional usage

- **Statistical arbitrage.** A pair or basket spread with H well below 0.5 is a candidate for mean-reversion trading. Use it alongside, not instead of, a cointegration or ADF test.
- **Regime filters.** A rolling H separates trending from choppy periods for momentum versus reversal strategies.
- **Volatility research.** Realised-volatility series show H around 0.1, the "rough volatility" finding of Gatheral, Jaisson and Rosenbaum (2018).

## Pitfalls

- R/S must be applied to returns, not price levels. Applied to a price series, it returns values near 1 that mean nothing.
- Classical R/S is biased upward in small samples. On 4,096 i.i.d. normal returns the code below returns about 0.55, not 0.50. Use the Anis-Lloyd/Peters correction or DFA, and compare against a shuffled-series baseline.
- Estimates are noisy and sensitive to the range of window sizes. Report confidence intervals, for example from a block bootstrap, before trading on a value of 0.45.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/hurst-exponent/hurst-exponent.py

```python
import numpy as np

def hurst_rs(returns, min_n: int = 16) -> float:
    """Hurst exponent by rescaled-range (R/S) analysis.
    Input: a series of returns/increments, NOT price levels."""
    x = np.asarray(returns, dtype=float)
    N = len(x)
    sizes = np.unique(np.floor(np.logspace(np.log10(min_n),
                                           np.log10(N // 2), 20)).astype(int))
    rs = []
    for n in sizes:
        k = N // n
        seg = x[: k * n].reshape(k, n)
        dev = np.cumsum(seg - seg.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True), axis=1)
        R = dev.max(axis=1) - dev.min(axis=1)
        S = seg.std(axis=1, ddof=0)
        ok = S > 0
        rs.append(np.mean(R[ok] / S[ok]))
    H, _ = np.polyfit(np.log(sizes), np.log(rs), 1)
    return float(H)

def hurst_lag_var(log_price, max_lag: int = 100) -> float:
    """Hurst from scaling of lagged differences: std(x[t+tau]-x[t]) ~ tau^H.
    Input: log price levels."""
    x = np.asarray(log_price, dtype=float)
    lags = np.arange(2, max_lag)
    tau = [np.std(x[l:] - x[:-l]) for l in lags]
    H, _ = np.polyfit(np.log(lags), np.log(tau), 1)
    return float(H)
```

## FAQ

**What Hurst value indicates mean reversion?**

H below 0.5. Values near 0.5 are consistent with a random walk; small deviations are often estimator bias rather than tradable structure.

## Related

- [Order Flow Imbalance (OFI)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/ofi/)
- [Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) Test](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/adf-test/)
- [Cointegration (Engle-Granger & Johansen)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/cointegration/)

# Information Coefficient (IC)

> The cross-sectional correlation between a factor's values and subsequent asset returns. Rank IC, its mean and ICIR are the standard first test of whether an alpha factor predicts returns.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/information-coefficient/

Category: Factor Research & Alpha Evaluation. Term ID: `information-coefficient`.

## Definition

The information coefficient is the correlation, computed across assets on one date, between a factor's values and the returns those assets earn over the following holding period. Rank IC uses Spearman rank correlation, which is robust to outliers. A factor is judged on the time series of its IC: its mean, its stability (ICIR) and its statistical significance.

## Formula

```
IC_t      = corr( f_{i,t} , r_{i,t→t+h} )        across assets i on date t
Rank IC_t = corr( rank f_{i,t} , rank r_{i,t→t+h} )   (Spearman)

Mean IC   = (1/n) Σ_t IC_t
ICIR      = mean(IC) / std(IC)
t-stat    ≈ ICIR · √(n / h)        h-period overlapping returns, n dates

Fundamental law (Grinold):  IR ≈ IC · √breadth
```

## Institutional usage

- **Factor screening.** Rank IC is the first filter in most factor libraries. As a rough guide for daily-rebalanced equity factors, a mean rank IC of 0.02–0.05 with ICIR above about 0.5 is worth further work, subject to turnover and costs.
- **Decay analysis.** Computing IC for horizons h = 1, 5, 10, 20 shows how fast a signal decays, which sets the rebalance frequency.
- **Factor weighting.** Rolling mean IC or ICIR is a common input to dynamic factor weighting and to the expected-return scaling in mean-variance optimisation.

## Pitfalls

- **Look-ahead.** Forward returns must start after the signal is known. For A-shares, a factor computed at the close of t can only be traded at t+1 because of T+1 settlement and order timing, so the code defaults to `lag=1`.
- **Untradeable names.** Suspended stocks, and A-share stocks that open at limit-up (for buys) or limit-down (for sells), should be masked out. Otherwise IC overstates what can actually be captured.
- **Overlapping horizons.** With h > 1 consecutive IC values share returns, so the naive t-stat is inflated. Use the √(n/h) adjustment shown here or Newey-West standard errors.
- **Size and industry exposure.** A factor that is mostly a small-cap or sector bet will show high IC in some regimes. Neutralise against size and industry before judging it.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy, pandas. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/information-coefficient/information-coefficient.py

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def forward_returns(close: pd.DataFrame, horizon: int = 1, lag: int = 1) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Forward return aligned to the signal date.
    close: dates x assets. A signal computed at the close of t is traded at t+lag
    (lag=1 suits A-share T+1 execution) and held for `horizon` periods."""
    return close.shift(-lag - horizon) / close.shift(-lag) - 1

def information_coefficient(factor: pd.DataFrame, fwd_ret: pd.DataFrame,
                            method: str = "rank", min_obs: int = 20) -> pd.Series:
    """Cross-sectional IC per date, fully vectorised (no per-date loop).
    method="rank" gives Spearman rank IC; "pearson" gives normal IC."""
    f, r = factor.align(fwd_ret, join="inner")
    valid = f.notna() & r.notna()
    f, r = f.where(valid), r.where(valid)
    if method == "rank":
        f, r = f.rank(axis=1), r.rank(axis=1)
    f = f.sub(f.mean(axis=1), axis=0)
    r = r.sub(r.mean(axis=1), axis=0)
    ic = (f * r).sum(axis=1) / np.sqrt((f ** 2).sum(axis=1) * (r ** 2).sum(axis=1))
    return ic.where(valid.sum(axis=1) >= min_obs)

def ic_summary(ic: pd.Series, horizon: int = 1) -> dict:
    """Mean IC, ICIR and an approximate t-stat. Overlapping horizons share
    information, so the effective sample size is taken as n / horizon."""
    ic = ic.dropna()
    n, m, s = len(ic), ic.mean(), ic.std(ddof=1)
    return {"n": n, "mean_ic": m, "ic_std": s, "icir": m / s,
            "t_stat": m / s * np.sqrt(n / horizon), "hit_rate": (ic > 0).mean()}
```

## FAQ

**What is a good IC value?**

For daily or weekly equity factors, a mean rank IC around 0.03–0.05 is typically considered meaningful, and ICIR above 0.5 indicates a stable signal. Values much higher than 0.1 on broad universes usually point to look-ahead bias or a data error.

**Should I use rank IC or Pearson IC?**

Rank IC is the default because it is robust to outliers and to the non-normal cross-section of returns. Pearson IC is closer to what a linear model captures and is useful when factor values are already standardised and winsorised.

- [Hurst Exponent (H)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/hurst-exponent/)
- [Volume-Weighted Average Price (VWAP)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vwap/)
- [Vectorised Daily Backtest with A-share Trading Constraints](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/vectorized-backtest/)
- [Amihud Illiquidity Measure (ILLIQ)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/amihud-illiquidity/)

# Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) Test

> A unit-root test that checks whether a time series is non-stationary. In stat-arb it is the standard check that a spread mean-reverts before it is traded.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/adf-test/

Category: Time Series & Stat-Arb. Term ID: `adf-test`.

## Definition

The Augmented Dickey-Fuller test asks whether a series has a unit root, meaning shocks never decay and the series wanders like a random walk. The null hypothesis is a unit root (non-stationary). A sufficiently negative test statistic rejects it in favour of a stationary, mean-reverting series. Lagged differences are added to the regression to absorb serial correlation.

## Formula

```
Δy_t = α + β·t + γ·y_{t−1} + Σ_{i=1..p} δ_i·Δy_{t−i} + ε_t

H0: γ = 0 (unit root)     H1: γ < 0 (stationary)
ADF statistic = γ̂ / se(γ̂)     → compare with Dickey-Fuller (MacKinnon) critical values,
                                  NOT Student-t
Large-sample critical values, constant only:  1% −3.43   5% −2.86   10% −2.57

Mean-reversion half-life (from Δy_t = a + g·y_{t−1}):  HL = ln 2 / −ln(1 + g)
```

## Institutional usage

- **Pairs and basket spreads.** A spread is traded only if ADF rejects a unit root. The half-life then sets the holding period and the look-back for the rolling mean and standard deviation of the z-score.
- **Model hygiene.** Regressing one non-stationary series on another gives spurious R² and t-stats. Test levels first, and difference or use cointegration methods when a unit root is present.
- **Feature engineering.** Testing candidate features for stationarity before feeding them to ML models avoids features whose distribution drifts out of the training range.

## Pitfalls

- **Low power.** With a few hundred observations, ADF often cannot tell a slowly mean-reverting series (AR coefficient 0.98) from a random walk. Failing to reject is not evidence of a unit root. Pair it with KPSS, whose null is the reverse.
- **Deterministic terms matter.** Including a trend when there is none, or omitting one that exists, shifts the critical values and the conclusion. Use `"c"` for spreads and `"ct"` only for trending series.
- **Structural breaks.** A level shift, such as a regime change or an index inclusion, makes a stationary series look non-stationary (Perron, 1989).
- **Estimated spreads.** If the series is a regression residual, ordinary ADF p-values are too optimistic. Use residual-based critical values: see [cointegration](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/cointegration/).
- **Multiple testing.** Screening thousands of A-share pairs at 5% yields hundreds of false positives. Adjust the threshold, or require out-of-sample confirmation.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy, statsmodels. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/adf-test/adf-test.py

```python
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller

def adf_stat(y, lags: int = 1) -> float:
    """ADF t-statistic with a constant, by plain OLS (for understanding).
    Regression: dy_t = a + g*y_{t-1} + sum_{i=1..lags} b_i*dy_{t-i} + e_t ;  returns t(g)."""
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    dy = np.diff(y)
    T = len(dy) - lags
    X = [np.ones(T), y[lags:-1]]
    X += [dy[lags - i:-i] for i in range(1, lags + 1)]
    X = np.column_stack(X)
    target = dy[lags:]
    beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, target, rcond=None)
    resid = target - X @ beta
    s2 = resid @ resid / (T - X.shape[1])
    se = np.sqrt(s2 * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)[1, 1])
    return float(beta[1] / se)

def adf_test(y, regression: str = "c") -> dict:
    """Production test: lag order by AIC and MacKinnon p-values via statsmodels.
    regression: "c" constant, "ct" constant + trend, "n" none."""
    y = np.asarray(y, float)
    try:   # statsmodels >= 0.15 lets us pin the classic tuple return
        res = adfuller(y, regression=regression, autolag="AIC", result_object=False)
    except TypeError:
        res = adfuller(y, regression=regression, autolag="AIC")
    return {"stat": res[0], "pvalue": res[1], "lags": res[2], "nobs": res[3], "crit": res[4]}

def half_life(y) -> float:
    """Mean-reversion half-life in periods from dy_t = a + g*y_{t-1}: ln(2) / -ln(1+g).
    Returns inf if the series is not mean-reverting (g >= 0)."""
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(y) - 1), y[:-1]])
    g = np.linalg.lstsq(X, np.diff(y), rcond=None)[0][1]
    return float(np.log(2) / -np.log1p(g)) if g < -1e-10 else float("inf")
```

## FAQ

**What is the difference between the ADF and KPSS tests?**

They reverse the hypotheses. ADF's null is a unit root (non-stationary); KPSS's null is stationarity. Rejecting ADF and failing to reject KPSS together is the strongest evidence of stationarity; conflicting results usually mean the sample is too short or the series is near a unit root.

**Which p-value threshold should I use for pairs selection?**

5% is conventional for a single test, but screening many pairs inflates false discoveries. Use a stricter threshold such as 1%, a false-discovery-rate correction, or confirm stationarity on a later out-of-sample window before trading.

- [Hurst Exponent (H)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/hurst-exponent/)
- [Fast Rolling Mean, Std, Beta and Z-score with Numba](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/rolling-window-numba/)

# Cointegration (Engle-Granger & Johansen)

> Two or more non-stationary price series are cointegrated when some linear combination of them is stationary. This is the statistical basis of pairs and basket trading.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/cointegration/

Category: Time Series & Stat-Arb. Term ID: `cointegration`.

## Definition

Cointegration means that individually non-stationary series share a common stochastic trend, so a weighted combination of them (the spread) is stationary and mean-reverts. The Engle-Granger two-step method tests one pair through a regression residual. The Johansen method tests several series at once and estimates how many independent cointegrating relationships exist.

## Formula

```
Engle-Granger (two steps):
  1. y_t = α + β·x_t + u_t            (OLS; β = hedge ratio)
  2. ADF on û_t with residual-based MacKinnon critical values
     (2 series, constant: 1% −3.90   5% −3.34   10% −3.04)

Johansen (VECM):
  Δy_t = Π·y_{t−1} + Σ_{i=1..k} Γ_i·Δy_{t−i} + ε_t ,   rank(Π) = r cointegrating vectors
  Trace statistic for H0: rank ≤ r :  λ_trace(r) = −T · Σ_{i=r+1..n} ln(1 − λ̂_i)
```

## Institutional usage

- **Pairs trading.** Go long the spread when its z-score is low and short when it is high. Size the legs with the hedge ratio β.
- **Basket and index arbitrage.** Johansen finds stationary portfolios across three or more assets, for example an ETF against its largest constituents.
- **Cross-market spreads.** Examples include A/H dual-listed shares, futures calendar spreads, and commodity crack or crush spreads.

## Pitfalls

- **Wrong p-values.** Running a plain ADF on an estimated residual overstates significance, because OLS already minimised the residual variance. In the test for this page, an unrelated pair gets p = 0.11 from plain ADF but p = 0.27 from the correct residual-based test.
- **Asymmetry.** Regressing y on x and x on y give different hedge ratios and can give different conclusions. Johansen is symmetric.
- **Unstable hedge ratios.** A β estimated once drifts over time. Re-estimate on a rolling window, or let β vary with a Kalman filter.
- **Correlation is not cointegration.** Two stocks can have highly correlated returns yet drift apart without bound in price.
- **A-share implementation.** Short legs depend on margin-lending availability (融券), which is limited and was further restricted from 2023. Many A-share pair strategies are therefore run as long-only relative-value switches or hedged with index futures.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy, statsmodels. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/cointegration/cointegration.py

```python
import warnings
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import coint
from statsmodels.tsa.vector_ar.vecm import coint_johansen

def engle_granger(y, x) -> dict:
    """Two-step Engle-Granger test of y ~ a + b*x.
    Uses residual-based MacKinnon critical values (statsmodels.coint), NOT the
    ordinary ADF p-value, which is too lenient for an estimated spread."""
    y, x = np.asarray(y, float), np.asarray(x, float)
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(x), x])
    (a, b), *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
    stat, p, crit = coint(y, x, trend="c", autolag="AIC")
    return {"alpha": a, "hedge_ratio": b, "spread": y - a - b * x,
            "stat": stat, "pvalue": p, "crit": crit}

def johansen(prices, det_order: int = 0, k_ar_diff: int = 1) -> dict:
    """Johansen trace test for an (T x n) price matrix.
    det_order: -1 none, 0 constant, 1 trend. Returns the cointegration rank
    at 95% and the first cointegrating vector (normalised on asset 0)."""
    with warnings.catch_warnings():  # recent NumPy: harmless ComplexWarning inside statsmodels
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore", np.exceptions.ComplexWarning)
        res = coint_johansen(np.asarray(prices, float), det_order, k_ar_diff)
    trace, cv95 = res.lr1, res.cvt[:, 1]
    rank = 0
    while rank < len(trace) and trace[rank] > cv95[rank]:
        rank += 1
    vec = np.real(res.evec[:, 0] / res.evec[0, 0])
    return {"rank": rank, "trace": trace, "cv95": cv95, "weights": vec}
```

## FAQ

**Should I use Engle-Granger or Johansen?**

Engle-Granger is simple and fine for a single pair, but its result depends on which series is the dependent variable and it finds at most one relationship. Johansen handles three or more series, is symmetric and estimates the number of cointegrating vectors, at the cost of sensitivity to lag length and deterministic-term choices.

**How is cointegration different from correlation?**

Correlation measures co-movement of returns over a window; cointegration is about the price levels staying tied together over time. Highly correlated stocks can drift apart permanently, while cointegrated ones are pulled back to an equilibrium spread.

- [Hurst Exponent (H)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/hurst-exponent/)
- [Fast Rolling Mean, Std, Beta and Z-score with Numba](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/rolling-window-numba/)

# Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES)

> VaR is the loss threshold that is exceeded only with a given small probability. Expected Shortfall is the average loss in that tail. Both are standard risk limits; ES is what Basel FRTB uses for market risk capital.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/var-expected-shortfall/

Category: Risk Management. Term ID: `var-expected-shortfall`.

## Definition

Value at Risk at confidence level α is the loss that is not exceeded with probability α over a given horizon. Expected Shortfall (also called CVaR) is the average loss given that the loss exceeds VaR. ES therefore accounts for how bad the tail is, not only where it starts. Unlike VaR, it is a coherent risk measure (subadditive).

## Formula

```
VaR_α = −q_{1−α}(r)                         (q = quantile of returns)
ES_α  = −E[ r | r ≤ q_{1−α}(r) ]

Normal:          VaR = −(μ + σ·z),   ES = −(μ − σ·φ(z)/(1−α)),   z = Φ⁻¹(1−α)
Cornish-Fisher:  z_cf = z + (z²−1)S/6 + (z³−3z)K/24 − (2z³−5z)S²/36
                 (S = skewness, K = excess kurtosis)

Kupiec POF backtest (x exceptions in n days, p = 1−α, p̂ = x/n):
  LR = −2·ln[ (1−p)^{n−x} p^x / ((1−p̂)^{n−x} p̂^x) ]  ~ χ²(1)
```

## Institutional usage

- **Risk limits and reporting.** Daily 99% VaR is the classic desk limit. Basel FRTB replaced it with 97.5% ES for market-risk capital because ES captures tail severity.
- **Backtesting.** Regulators and risk teams count VaR exceptions and run the Kupiec test. Too many exceptions mean the model understates risk.
- **Strategy evaluation.** Historical VaR and ES of a backtest's daily returns are reported alongside Sharpe and max drawdown. The [performance calculator](https://quantcore-labs.com/tools/performance-analytics/) computes them from a pasted equity curve.

## Pitfalls

- **Normal VaR understates fat tails.** On simulated Student-t (4 degrees of freedom) returns, 99% normal VaR is 3.26% against a historical 3.75%, and normal ES misses by even more (3.74% against 5.12%).
- **Cornish-Fisher can overshoot.** The expansion is only valid for moderate skew and kurtosis. On the same t(4) sample it gives 6.03%, far above the true quantile. Prefer historical or filtered-historical methods for heavy tails.
- **Sample size.** A 99% historical VaR from 250 days rests on about 2.5 observations. Use longer windows, or 97.5% ES, which averages more points.
- **√h scaling.** Multiplying 1-day VaR by √10 assumes i.i.d. returns. Volatility clustering and autocorrelation break it.
- **A-share price limits.** The ±10% daily limit (±20% on ChiNext and STAR, ±5% for ST) truncates observed daily losses. Consecutive limit-down days then produce multi-day losses far beyond the 1-day historical VaR.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy, scipy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/var-expected-shortfall/var-expected-shortfall.py

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm, chi2

def var_es(returns, alpha: float = 0.99, method: str = "historical") -> tuple:
    """One-period VaR and Expected Shortfall as positive loss fractions.
    method: "historical" | "normal" | "cornish-fisher" (skew/kurtosis-adjusted
    quantile; returns ES = nan because the expansion defines no tail mean)."""
    r = np.asarray(returns, dtype=float)
    r = r[~np.isnan(r)]
    if method == "historical":
        q = np.quantile(r, 1 - alpha)
        return -q, -r[r <= q].mean()
    mu, sd = r.mean(), r.std(ddof=1)
    z = norm.ppf(1 - alpha)
    if method == "normal":
        return -(mu + sd * z), -(mu - sd * norm.pdf(z) / (1 - alpha))
    if method == "cornish-fisher":
        # VaR only: CF adjusts the quantile, it does not define a tail mean.
        x = (r - mu) / sd
        s, k = np.mean(x ** 3), np.mean(x ** 4) - 3
        zc = z + (z**2 - 1) * s / 6 + (z**3 - 3*z) * k / 24 - (2*z**3 - 5*z) * s**2 / 36
        return -(mu + sd * zc), float("nan")
    raise ValueError(method)

def kupiec_pof(returns, var_series, alpha: float = 0.99) -> dict:
    """Kupiec proportion-of-failures backtest. var_series: forecast VaR (positive)
    made BEFORE each return. H0: exception rate = 1 - alpha."""
    r, v = np.asarray(returns, float), np.asarray(var_series, float)
    n, x, p = len(r), int((r < -v).sum()), 1 - alpha
    ph = x / n
    ll0 = (n - x) * np.log(1 - p) + x * np.log(p)
    ll1 = (0.0 if x == n else (n - x) * np.log(1 - ph)) + (0.0 if x == 0 else x * np.log(ph))
    lr = -2 * (ll0 - ll1)
    return {"n": n, "exceptions": x, "expected": n * p, "lr": lr, "pvalue": 1 - chi2.cdf(lr, 1)}
```

## FAQ

**Should I use 95%, 99% or 97.5%?**

99% one-day VaR is the traditional trading-desk limit and Basel VaR standard; 97.5% ES is the Basel FRTB standard and is roughly comparable in level to 99% VaR under normality while being more stable to estimate. 95% is common for strategy reporting because it has more tail observations.

**Why is Expected Shortfall preferred to VaR?**

VaR says nothing about losses beyond the threshold and is not subadditive, so combining two portfolios can show higher VaR than the sum of their VaRs. ES averages the whole tail and is coherent, which makes it better for limits and capital allocation.

- [Vectorised Daily Backtest with A-share Trading Constraints](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/vectorized-backtest/)

# Amihud Illiquidity Measure (ILLIQ)

> The average absolute return per unit of traded value: how much the price moves for each yuan or dollar traded. It is a low-frequency price-impact proxy and a widely used liquidity factor.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/amihud-illiquidity/

Category: Execution & Market Microstructure. Term ID: `amihud-illiquidity`.

## Definition

Amihud (2002) illiquidity is the average, over a window of days, of the absolute daily return divided by the day's traded value. A high value means small amounts of trading move the price a lot. It needs only daily returns and turnover, so it can be computed for every stock over long histories. That makes it the standard low-frequency liquidity measure in asset-pricing research.

## Formula

```
ILLIQ_{i,T} = (1 / D_{i,T}) · Σ_{d ∈ T} |r_{i,d}| / VOLD_{i,d}  × scale

r_{i,d}    : daily return of stock i
VOLD_{i,d} : traded value that day (A-shares: 成交额 in yuan, not 成交量 in shares)
D_{i,T}    : number of valid trading days in window T (zero-turnover days excluded)
scale      : e.g. 10⁸ → |return| per 100 million yuan traded
```

## Institutional usage

- **Liquidity factor.** Illiquid stocks earn a return premium in many markets, and Amihud ILLIQ is the usual sort variable. It is a common factor in A-share multi-factor models, often in log form.
- **Capacity and cost estimates.** ILLIQ times the planned trade size gives a rough expected price move. This is used to cap position sizes in small-cap strategies.
- **Universe filters.** Excluding the most illiquid decile before backtesting avoids returns that could never be captured at scale.

## Pitfalls

- **Use value, not volume.** Dividing by share volume makes a ¥5 stock look far more liquid than a ¥500 stock with the same yuan turnover.
- **Suspensions.** Zero-turnover days give infinite ratios. The code drops them and requires a minimum number of valid days.
- **Price-limit days.** A stock that is locked at limit-up shows about a 10% move on tiny turnover, which creates extreme ILLIQ values. Winsorise, or exclude limit-locked days, and note that ChiNext and STAR moved to ±20% limits, so mixed-regime histories are not directly comparable.
- **Skew.** The cross-section spans several orders of magnitude. Use log(ILLIQ) or ranks in regressions and factor models.
- **Size proxy.** ILLIQ is strongly correlated with market cap. Neutralise against size before claiming a separate liquidity effect.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy, pandas. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/amihud-illiquidity/amihud-illiquidity.py

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def amihud(ret: pd.DataFrame, amount: pd.DataFrame, window: int = 20,
           min_days: int = 15, scale: float = 1e8) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Rolling Amihud illiquidity, dates x stocks, fully vectorised.
    ILLIQ = mean(|r_t| / amount_t) * scale over the window.
    amount: traded value in currency (A-shares: yuan turnover, 成交额), so with
    scale=1e8 the result reads as |return| per 100 million yuan traded.
    Zero-amount days (suspensions) are excluded rather than producing inf."""
    a = amount.where(amount > 0)
    daily = ret.abs() / a
    return daily.rolling(window, min_periods=min_days).mean() * scale

def amihud_monthly(ret: pd.DataFrame, amount: pd.DataFrame, scale: float = 1e8) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Original Amihud (2002) style: average within each calendar month."""
    daily = ret.abs() / amount.where(amount > 0)
    return daily.groupby(daily.index.to_period("M")).mean() * scale
```

## FAQ

**Why take the log of Amihud illiquidity?**

Raw ILLIQ is extremely right-skewed: the most illiquid stocks can be thousands of times the median. Log or rank transforms keep a few outliers from dominating regressions, factor portfolios and IC calculations.

**Monthly or rolling window?**

The original paper averages within each calendar month or year. A rolling 20-day window updates daily and suits trading signals; use at least 15 valid days so suspensions do not produce noisy values.

- [Volume-Weighted Average Price (VWAP)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vwap/)
- [Information Coefficient (IC)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/information-coefficient/)
- [Query Tick Data in Parquet with DuckDB](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/duckdb-parquet-ticks/)

# Volume-Synchronized Probability of Informed Trading (VPIN)

> An estimate of order-flow toxicity from the imbalance between buy and sell volume inside equal-volume buckets. It updates by volume, not by the clock.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vpin/

Category: Market Microstructure & Order Flow. Term ID: `vpin`.

## Definition

VPIN averages the absolute difference between buy volume and sell volume across the last n equal-volume buckets, and divides by the volume those buckets represent. Easley, López de Prado and O'Hara designed it as a high-frequency cousin of the probability of informed trading: a bucket is toxic when one side dominates. The measure does not classify trades by itself. Buy and sell volume are inputs, usually from a bulk-volume split or from an aggressor flag.

## Formula

```
V = target volume of each bucket
VPIN = Σ_{τ=1..n} |V^B_τ − V^S_τ| / (n · V)

If every bucket is exactly volume V and V^B + V^S = V, then 0 ≤ VPIN ≤ 1.
VPIN = 0: buy and sell volume match in every bucket
VPIN = 1: each bucket is entirely one side
```

## How desks use the number

- As a state variable for quoting: a higher reading means recent volume was more one-sided, so a market maker may widen or cut size. It is a description of the recent tape, not a forecast with a promised hit rate.
- The buckets are equal volume, not equal time. Build them with something like [volume bars](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/pandas-volume-bars/), then split each bar's volume into buy and sell.
- The daily structural model behind the same idea is [PIN](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/pin-informed-trading/). A price-impact slope on signed volume is [Kyle's lambda](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/kyles-lambda/).

## Pitfalls

- **Classification is the measurement.** Bulk-volume classification assigns a fraction of each bar to buy or sell from the price change. A different rule produces a different VPIN. Report the rule.
- **The denominator assumes equal buckets.** The code below rejects a row whose buy plus sell volume is not the stated bucket size. A partial last bucket should be dropped, not squeezed into the formula.
- **It is not a probability you can take to a risk limit without a model.** The name says probability. The calculation is a normalised imbalance. Mapping it onto the structural PIN parameters requires the model, not just the ratio.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy, pandas. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vpin/vpin.py

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def compute_vpin(volume_buckets: pd.DataFrame, bucket_size: float) -> float:
    """VPIN from equal-volume buckets with buy_vol and sell_vol columns.

    Each row must sum to bucket_size. The function does not classify trades.
    """
    if bucket_size <= 0:
        raise ValueError("bucket_size must be positive")
    buy = np.asarray(volume_buckets["buy_vol"], dtype=float)
    sell = np.asarray(volume_buckets["sell_vol"], dtype=float)
    if buy.shape != sell.shape or buy.size == 0:
        raise ValueError("need at least one buy/sell bucket")
    if np.any(buy < 0) or np.any(sell < 0):
        raise ValueError("volumes must be non-negative")
    total = buy + sell
    if np.max(np.abs(total - bucket_size)) > 1e-6 * bucket_size:
        raise ValueError("each bucket must sum to bucket_size; drop a partial tail")
    return float(np.abs(buy - sell).sum() / (buy.size * bucket_size))
```

## FAQ

**Is VPIN the same as PIN?**

No. PIN is a daily mixture model estimated by maximum likelihood from buy and sell counts. VPIN is a rolling volume-bucket imbalance that can be updated through the day. They share an author and an interpretation, not a formula.

**What is a high VPIN?**

The ratio is between 0 and 1 when buckets are well formed. How high is unusual depends on the symbol, the bucket size and the classification rule. Compare a name with its own history before comparing it with another name.

## Related

- [Probability of Informed Trading (PIN)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/pin-informed-trading/)
- [Kyle's Lambda](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/kyles-lambda/)
- [Equal-Volume Bars from a Trade Tape](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/pandas-volume-bars/)
- [Order Flow Imbalance (OFI)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/ofi/)

# Time-Weighted Average Price (TWAP)

> The arithmetic average of prices sampled on a regular clock. As a benchmark every interval counts once; as a schedule, a parent order is sliced evenly in time.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/twap/

Category: Execution & Market Microstructure. Term ID: `twap`.

## Definition

TWAP is the mean of a price series after it has been sampled at equal time intervals. Volume does not enter. A TWAP execution schedule therefore sends about the same quantity in each slice of the horizon, regardless of whether the market is busy. The benchmark form asks whether fills beat the average of those sampled prices.

## Formula

```
TWAP = (1 / N) Σ_{k=1..N} P_{t_k}

t_k equally spaced. P is the sample chosen for that slot (here: the last trade in the bin).

A TWAP schedule over horizon T with quantity Q sends about Q / N in each slice.
It does not target a fraction of market volume. That is participation rate.
```

## Benchmark versus schedule

- **Benchmark.** Sample the market on a clock and average it. The implementation below uses the last trade in each bin, which is one convention. The mean of all trades in the bin is another, and it is not TWAP in the strict equal-time sense because a busy bin would contribute more prints.
- **Schedule.** Child orders of equal size at equal times. This page does not size those children. Participation (percent of volume) is a different schedule: [participation rate](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/participation-rate/).
- [VWAP](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vwap/) weights the same trades by size, so it follows the volume curve. TWAP does not. Quiet minutes count as much as the close.

## Pitfalls

- **Sampling inside the bin matters.** Last trade, first trade, and the bin's VWAP answer different questions. Say which one the benchmark used.
- **A regular clock includes empty periods only if you define a price for them.** This function drops empty bins, so a halt does not create a slot. Forward-filling across a halt pretends a trade happened.
- **Easy to game, easy to be gamed.** A schedule that must finish a slice every minute will trade through a spread that a volume-aware schedule would wait out. The average is not a target to beat for its own sake.

## Python reference implementation

Requires pandas. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/twap/twap.py

```python
import pandas as pd

def calculate_twap(prices, freq="1min") -> float:
    """Arithmetic mean of regularly sampled prices.

    A Series with a DatetimeIndex is sampled by taking the last observation
    in each bin of width `freq`, dropping empty bins. Any other input is
    treated as already sampled, and the mean of its values is returned.
    """
    if not isinstance(prices, pd.Series):
        prices = pd.Series(prices, dtype="float64")
    if isinstance(prices.index, pd.DatetimeIndex):
        sampled = prices.sort_index().resample(freq).last().dropna()
    else:
        sampled = prices.dropna()
    if sampled.empty:
        raise ValueError("no prices to average")
    return float(sampled.mean())
```

## FAQ

**Why is TWAP not just the average of every trade?**

The average of every trade weights busy moments more heavily, because they contain more prints. That is closer to a trade-count weighted price. TWAP gives each time slot one vote, which is why the series is resampled before the mean.

**When would a TWAP schedule be a poor fit?**

When volume is concentrated, for example around an open, a close or an announcement. Equal time slices then trade a large fraction of the market when it is quiet and a small fraction when it is not. A VWAP or participation schedule follows the volume instead.

## Related

- [Volume-Weighted Average Price (VWAP)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vwap/)
- [Participation Rate (Percent of Volume)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/participation-rate/)
- [Arrival-Price Slippage](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/arrival-price/)

# Implementation Shortfall

> The gap between a paper portfolio filled at the decision price and the portfolio that was actually traded, including fees and the cost of shares that never got filled.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/implementation-shortfall/

Category: Execution & Transaction Cost Analysis. Term ID: `implementation-shortfall`.

## Definition

Perold's implementation shortfall compares two portfolios. The paper portfolio trades the full target at the price that was current when the decision was made. The real portfolio trades what was filled, at the prices that were filled, and pays fees. The difference is the shortfall. It splits into an execution component on the shares that traded and an opportunity component on the shares that did not. A positive number is a cost relative to the paper portfolio.

## Formula

```
side = +1 buy, −1 sell
filled = Σ q_i

execution  = side · Σ q_i (P_i − P_decision)
opportunity = side · (Q − filled) · (P_end − P_decision)
IS = execution + opportunity + fees

P_end is the price used to mark the unfilled remainder (often the close, or the price when the order was cancelled).
IS is in currency of the prices times quantities, not in basis points.
```

## Reading the two pieces

- **Execution cost** is what you paid, relative to the decision price, on shares that did trade. Buying above the decision price is a positive cost.
- **Opportunity cost** is the paper profit on shares you wanted and did not get. If the price runs away after a buy decision and you do not finish, that move is part of the shortfall even though no fill occurred.
- Arrival-price slippage ignores the unfilled part. It is the execution piece only, in basis points: [arrival price](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/arrival-price/). A schedule that balances the two pieces is the point of [Almgren-Chriss](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/almgren-chriss/).

## Pitfalls

- **The decision price has to be fixed before the order does anything.** Using the first fill, or the arrival mid after the child orders have already moved the book, understates the shortfall.
- **P_end is a choice.** Marking leftovers at the close and marking them at the cancel time are different costs. Write down which one.
- **Sign.** The formula returns a cost. A negative shortfall means the real portfolio beat the paper one. Do not flip the sign between buys and sells; `side` does that.
- **Fees sit outside the price.** Commission, stamp and financing belong in `fees`. Burying them in the fill price double-counts once someone also subtracts them from PnL.

## Python reference implementation

Requires standard library. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/implementation-shortfall/implementation-shortfall.py

```python
def implementation_shortfall(fills, decision_px, end_px, target_qty, side=1, fees=0.0) -> float:
    """Implementation shortfall in price-times-quantity units. Positive = cost.

    fills: iterable of (qty, price). side = +1 buy, -1 sell.
    Unfilled size is marked at end_px. qty is unsigned.
    """
    if side not in (1, -1):
        raise ValueError("side must be +1 (buy) or -1 (sell)")
    if target_qty < 0:
        raise ValueError("target_qty must be non-negative")
    filled = 0.0
    execution = 0.0
    for qty, price in fills:
        if qty < 0:
            raise ValueError("fill quantities must be non-negative")
        filled += qty
        execution += side * qty * (price - decision_px)
    if filled > target_qty + 1e-8:
        raise ValueError("filled quantity exceeds target")
    opportunity = side * (target_qty - filled) * (end_px - decision_px)
    return float(execution + opportunity + fees)
```

## FAQ

**Why charge a cost for shares that did not trade?**

The decision was to hold the target. Shares that never filled are still a difference between the paper portfolio and the real one. If the price then moves in the direction of the decision, that missed move is an opportunity cost; if it moves the other way, the unfilled part reduces the shortfall.

**Is a negative shortfall good?**

It means the real fills, leftovers and fees beat trading the full size at the decision price. It is a cost accounting identity, not a statement that the decision itself was a good one.

## Related

- [Arrival-Price Slippage](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/arrival-price/)
- [Volume-Weighted Average Price (VWAP)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vwap/)
- [Almgren-Chriss Optimal Execution Trajectory](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/almgren-chriss/)

# Arrival-Price Slippage

> Execution cost against the mid-price at the moment the order arrived, in basis points. Positive means the fills were worse than that mid.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/arrival-price/

Category: Execution & Transaction Cost Analysis. Term ID: `arrival-price`.

## Definition

The arrival price is the mid (or other pre-agreed reference) when the order reached the desk or the algorithm, before the order's own child trades. Slippage is the signed difference between the average fill and that reference, scaled to basis points. Buys are costly when the average fill is above the arrival mid. Sells are costly when it is below.

## Formula

```
slippage_bps = side · (P_avg − P_arrival) / P_arrival · 10^4

side = +1 buy, −1 sell
P_arrival is a mid, not the last trade, unless the policy explicitly says otherwise
Positive slippage = worse than the arrival price
```

## What it does and does not include

- It prices the shares that filled. It says nothing about shares that did not. That remainder is the opportunity term in [implementation shortfall](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/implementation-shortfall/).
- It does not know why the price moved. Impact, drift and spread are all inside the same basis-point number. A later decomposition can split them; this ratio cannot.
- [VWAP](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vwap/) slippage asks a different question: did you beat the market's own average, rather than the price at arrival.

## Pitfalls

- **Stamp the mid before you send.** Reconstructing arrival from the first child fill includes your own impact and makes the order look cheaper than it was.
- **Average fill has to be volume-weighted.** The mean of child-order limit prices is not the average execution price.
- **Basis points hide the currency.** 5 bp on a large notional is a large amount. Report both when the number goes into a cost report.

## Python reference implementation

Requires standard library. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/arrival-price/arrival-price.py

```python
def arrival_slippage_bps(avg_exec_px, arrival_mid, side=1) -> float:
    """Signed execution cost versus the arrival mid, in basis points.

    side = +1 buy, -1 sell. Positive means worse than the arrival mid.
    """
    if arrival_mid <= 0:
        raise ValueError("arrival_mid must be positive")
    if side not in (1, -1):
        raise ValueError("side must be +1 (buy) or -1 (sell)")
    return float(side * (avg_exec_px - arrival_mid) / arrival_mid * 1e4)
```

## FAQ

**Why use the mid instead of the last trade?**

The last trade is whichever side last crossed the spread, so it sits half a spread away from a price you could have notionally dealt at on average. The mid is the usual pre-trade reference. If the policy uses the near touch or the last trade, the function still applies, but the input is no longer a mid and the name should say so.

**Does a negative number mean the execution was good?**

It means the average fill beat the arrival reference, after the sign for buy or sell. It does not include unfilled quantity, fees or whether the arrival price itself was a sensible time to trade.

## Related

- [Implementation Shortfall](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/implementation-shortfall/)
- [Volume-Weighted Average Price (VWAP)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vwap/)
- [Time-Weighted Average Price (TWAP)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/twap/)

# Participation Rate (Percent of Volume)

> The fraction of market volume an order takes over an interval. A percent-of-volume schedule sets each child order to that fraction of the volume just observed, capped by what is left.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/participation-rate/

Category: Execution & Market Microstructure. Term ID: `participation-rate`.

## Definition

Participation rate, or POV, is own volume divided by market volume over the same interval. A POV algorithm watches the market print, and sends a child quantity equal to a target fraction of that print, without exceeding the residual parent quantity. The target is a fraction of volume, not a clock and not a forecast of the day's volume curve.

## Formula

```
POV = V_own / V_market

Child quantity for one interval, given volume V printed in that interval:
  q = min(Q_remaining, ρ · V)

ρ is the target rate as a fraction (0.10 means ten percent of volume).
The child does not look ahead at volume that has not printed.
```

## How the schedule behaves

- Busy intervals produce larger children. Quiet intervals produce smaller ones. The order slows down when the market does, which a [TWAP](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/twap/) slice will not.
- It does not finish by a deadline. If volume dries up, quantity is left over. A horizon with a hard end needs a different schedule, such as [Almgren-Chriss](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/almgren-chriss/) or VWAP with a residual sweep.
- The realised rate is own fills over market volume, which includes your own prints if they are in the tape. Subtracting them is a policy choice and changes the number.

## Pitfalls

- **ρ is a fraction.** Passing 10 thinking it means 10 percent requests ten times market volume. The code treats 10 as 1000 percent and will try to take all remaining quantity.
- **The cap is the remaining parent, not a market-impact model.** min(remaining, ρ·V) does not estimate how far the child moves the price. Impact still scales with participation; this function only sizes the child.
- **Which volume.** Lit continuous volume, auction volume and odd-lot volume are different denominators. The caller passes the volume number; the function does not classify prints.

## Python reference implementation

Requires standard library. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/participation-rate/participation-rate.py

```python
def pov_child_qty(market_vol_interval, target_rate, remaining_qty) -> float:
    """Child quantity for a percent-of-volume slice.

    target_rate is a fraction of market volume (0.1 = 10%). The result is
    never larger than remaining_qty, and is zero when there is nothing to do.
    """
    if market_vol_interval < 0 or remaining_qty < 0:
        raise ValueError("volumes must be non-negative")
    if target_rate < 0:
        raise ValueError("target_rate must be non-negative")
    return float(min(remaining_qty, target_rate * market_vol_interval))
```

## FAQ

**Is participation the same as POV?**

POV (percent of volume) is the schedule that tries to keep participation near a target. Participation rate is the realised or target ratio itself. People use the two names for both the ratio and the algorithm; the formula on this page is the ratio, and the function is the child size that targets it.

**What rate is reasonable?**

There is no universal rate. Higher participation finishes sooner and usually moves the price more. The function does not choose ρ. It only converts a chosen rate and an observed volume into a child quantity.

## Related

- [Time-Weighted Average Price (TWAP)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/twap/)
- [Volume-Weighted Average Price (VWAP)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vwap/)
- [Almgren-Chriss Optimal Execution Trajectory](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/almgren-chriss/)

# Almgren-Chriss Optimal Execution Trajectory

> A deterministic schedule that liquidates a position by a fixed horizon, trading off temporary market impact against the variance of the remaining inventory. This page uses the continuous-time trajectory with permanent impact set to zero.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/almgren-chriss/

Category: Execution & Market Impact. Term ID: `almgren-chriss`.

## Definition

Almgren and Chriss (2000) choose a trading path that finishes a position by time T. Trading faster pays more temporary impact and less price risk, because the inventory is held for less time. The risk aversion λ sets that tradeoff. With linear temporary impact, no permanent impact, and arithmetic Brownian motion, the inventory that remains at time t is a hyperbolic sine of the time left. The path is a plan computed from volatility, impact and risk aversion. It is not a guarantee of the cost, and it is not an order.

## Formula

```
Inventory remaining (permanent impact taken as 0):

  x(t) = X · sinh(κ (T − t)) / sinh(κ T)
  κ = sqrt(λ σ² / η)

X     initial position (signed)
η     temporary-impact coefficient (cost ∝ η · speed² in the standard linear model)
σ     absolute price volatility
λ     risk aversion on inventory variance
T     horizon

As λ → 0 (or σ → 0), κ → 0 and x(t) → X · (T − t) / T, a straight line.
Trades are the decreases of x. x(0) = X and x(T) = 0.
```

## What the shape means

- Low risk aversion gives a near-linear liquidation: equal amounts of inventory per unit time, close to a [TWAP](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/twap/) schedule in trade time.
- High risk aversion sells (or buys) more at the start, because holding the inventory is what the objective penalises. The temporary-impact bill is accepted in exchange for less variance.
- The cost the path is balancing is the same object as [implementation shortfall](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/implementation-shortfall/): impact paid now versus the risk of still being in the position later.

## Pitfalls

- **This is the no-permanent-impact slice of the model.** The 2000 paper also has a permanent impact coefficient. It shifts the expected cost but, in their framework, not the optimal trajectory. Do not quote this κ as the full model if you have estimated a permanent term and intend to use a different objective.
- **σ, η and λ have to share units.** σ is absolute price volatility per unit time if the impact is in price, not in return. A return volatility plugged in beside a price impact produces a nonsense κ.
- **The path is open-loop.** It does not react to volume, spread or a signal. A [participation](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/participation-rate/) schedule does the opposite: it reacts to volume and does not promise a finish time.
- **Sinh overflows for large κT.** The implementation uses a ratio of exponentials and switches to the straight line when κT is tiny.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/almgren-chriss/almgren-chriss.py

```python
import numpy as np

def almgren_chriss_trajectory(X, T, n, sigma, eta, risk_aversion):
    """Inventory remaining on n equal steps from 0 to T, including both endpoints.

    Permanent impact is taken as zero. risk_aversion = 0 (or sigma = 0) returns
    the straight-line schedule. X may be signed.
    """
    if T <= 0 or int(n) < 1:
        raise ValueError("T must be positive and n at least 1")
    if eta <= 0 or sigma < 0 or risk_aversion < 0:
        raise ValueError("eta must be positive; sigma and risk_aversion non-negative")
    t = np.linspace(0.0, float(T), int(n) + 1)
    if risk_aversion == 0 or sigma == 0:
        return X * (T - t) / T
    kappa = np.sqrt(risk_aversion * sigma ** 2 / eta)
    if kappa * T < 1e-8:
        return X * (T - t) / T
    # sinh(κ(T-t)) / sinh(κT) = exp(a-b) * (1 - exp(-2a)) / (1 - exp(-2b))
    a = kappa * (T - t)
    b = kappa * T
    ratio = np.exp(a - b) * (1.0 - np.exp(-2.0 * a)) / (1.0 - np.exp(-2.0 * b))
    return X * ratio
```

## FAQ

**Why is the zero-risk path a straight line?**

With no penalty on inventory variance, the objective only punishes trading speed, and the cheapest way to finish by T with linear temporary impact is to trade at a constant speed. Any front-loading would pay more impact without a benefit the objective recognises.

**Does the trajectory include permanent impact?**

No. κ above uses temporary impact η only. In the original linear model, adding permanent impact changes expected cost and does not change this particular trajectory. If your impact model is not that one, do not reuse the path unchanged.

## Related

- [Implementation Shortfall](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/implementation-shortfall/)
- [Participation Rate (Percent of Volume)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/participation-rate/)
- [Time-Weighted Average Price (TWAP)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/twap/)

# Kyle's Lambda

> The slope of price changes on signed order flow. A larger lambda means the same signed volume moves the price more, which is the usual reduced-form reading of a less liquid market.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/kyles-lambda/

Category: Market Microstructure & Order Flow. Term ID: `kyles-lambda`.

## Definition

In Kyle's 1985 model, competitive market makers set price impact so that the price is the conditional expectation of value given the net order flow. The impact coefficient is lambda. Empirically, lambda is estimated as the OLS slope of a price change on signed volume over a chosen interval. The intercept absorbs drift. This page is that regression, not a maximum-likelihood estimate of the structural model.

## Formula

```
ΔP_t = α + λ · SignedVolume_t + ε_t

λ = Cov(ΔP, SignedVolume) / Var(SignedVolume)

SignedVolume > 0 means net buying. The sign convention has to match ΔP:
a buy-driven uptick is positive volume with a positive price change.
Units of λ are price per unit of volume.
```

## What the slope is used for

- Comparing liquidity across names or across time: a higher λ is more impact per unit of signed volume. Scale volume before comparing a high-priced name with a low-priced one, or work in returns and turnover instead of raw price and shares.
- As a cost input. A parent order of signed size Q has an impact term on the order of λ·Q in this linear model, before temporary spread and fees. That is a sketch, not a cost forecast.
- Related tape measures: [VPIN](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vpin/) (volume imbalance), [OFI](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/ofi/) (quote updates) and [Amihud](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/amihud-illiquidity/) (daily |return| over value).

## Pitfalls

- **Trade signs.** A wrong aggressor flag flips the slope's sign. Quote-rule labels from an [as-of join](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/polars-asof-join-quotes/) are an estimate of the sign, not the exchange flag.
- **Horizon.** Lambda on one-second bins and lambda on daily bins are different parameters. Impact decays; a longer bin lets some of it come back and the slope falls.
- **Endogeneity.** Signed volume and the price change are determined together. OLS is the reduced form people report. It is not, by itself, the structural Kyle lambda.
- **Zero flow variance.** A window with no variation in signed volume has no slope. The function raises rather than returning a silent NaN from a degenerate fit.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/kyles-lambda/kyles-lambda.py

```python
import numpy as np

def kyles_lambda(price_changes, signed_volume) -> float:
    """OLS slope of price changes on signed volume, with an intercept."""
    x = np.asarray(signed_volume, dtype=float)
    y = np.asarray(price_changes, dtype=float)
    if x.shape != y.shape or x.ndim != 1 or x.size < 2:
        raise ValueError("need at least two aligned observations")
    xc = x - x.mean()
    var = float(xc @ xc)
    if var <= 0:
        raise ValueError("signed volume has zero variance")
    yc = y - y.mean()
    return float((xc @ yc) / var)
```

## FAQ

**Why include an intercept?**

The price can drift over the sample for reasons other than the signed flow in the regression. Without an intercept, that drift is forced into the slope. OLS with an intercept is also what np.polyfit of degree 1 estimates.

**Can lambda be negative?**

In the model, no: informed buying pushes the price up. In a sample, yes, if the signs are noisy or the window is short. A negative estimate is a warning about the regression, not a negative liquidity.

## Related

- [Volume-Synchronized Probability of Informed Trading (VPIN)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vpin/)
- [Order Flow Imbalance (OFI)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/ofi/)
- [Amihud Illiquidity Measure (ILLIQ)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/amihud-illiquidity/)
- [Attach the Prevailing Quote to Each Trade](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/polars-asof-join-quotes/)
