# Probability of Informed Trading (PIN)

> The share of trading that the Easley-Kiefer-O'Hara-Paperman model attributes to informed traders, given the chance of an information event and the arrival rates of informed and uninformed orders.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/pin-informed-trading/

Category: Market Microstructure & Order Flow. Term ID: `pin-informed-trading`.

## Definition

PIN is the model's probability that the next trade comes from an informed trader. An information event occurs with probability α. If it does, informed orders arrive at rate μ, on the buy side or the sell side according to the news. Uninformed buys and sells arrive at rates ε_b and ε_s whether or not there was news. PIN is the expected informed arrival divided by the expected total arrival. Estimating α, μ and the epsilons is a separate maximum-likelihood problem on daily buy and sell counts. This page evaluates the formula once those parameters are in hand. It does not fit them.

## Formula

```
PIN = α μ / (α μ + ε_b + ε_s)

α   probability of an information event, in [0, 1]
μ   arrival rate of informed traders when there is news
ε_b, ε_s  arrival rates of uninformed buyers and sellers

The denominator is the expected rate of all trades.
PIN is between 0 and 1 when the inputs are valid.
```

## What you do with the parameters

- Once a fit exists, PIN summarises it in one number. Comparing PIN across names is comparing those fits, so the count data, the day length and the optimiser have to be the same kind of exercise.
- The high-frequency imbalance that is often used in place of a daily fit is [VPIN](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vpin/). It does not estimate α and μ.
- A price-impact slope is a different object again: [Kyle's lambda](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/kyles-lambda/).

## Pitfalls

- **The formula is not the estimator.** The likelihood is a mixture of Poissons and it has well known local maxima, including the buy-sell symmetry of the original model. A closed form for PIN does not remove that. This function will happily turn a bad fit into a precise-looking ratio.
- **Buys and sells must be classified first.** The classic papers use a trade-classification algorithm. Different signs, different PIN.
- **Zero total intensity.** If every rate is zero the ratio is undefined. The function raises.

## Python reference implementation

Requires standard library. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/pin-informed-trading/pin-informed-trading.py

```python
def pin(alpha, mu, eps_b, eps_s) -> float:
    """PIN = alpha*mu / (alpha*mu + eps_b + eps_s). Evaluates parameters; does not estimate them."""
    alpha, mu, eps_b, eps_s = float(alpha), float(mu), float(eps_b), float(eps_s)
    if not 0.0 <= alpha <= 1.0:
        raise ValueError("alpha must be in [0, 1]")
    if mu < 0 or eps_b < 0 or eps_s < 0:
        raise ValueError("arrival rates must be non-negative")
    informed = alpha * mu
    total = informed + eps_b + eps_s
    if total <= 0:
        raise ValueError("total arrival rate must be positive")
    return informed / total
```

## FAQ

**Why doesn't this page estimate PIN?**

The estimate is a constrained maximum-likelihood fit of a Poisson mixture, and the likelihood is not concave. A short optimiser pasted into a glossary page would look authoritative and land in local maxima. The page publishes the map from parameters to PIN, which is the part with a closed form.

**What does a PIN of 0.2 mean?**

Inside the model, one trade in five is from an informed trader, at the estimated arrival rates. Outside the model it is only as meaningful as the fit. It is not a probability you can read off the tape without estimating the parameters.

## Related

- [Volume-Synchronized Probability of Informed Trading (VPIN)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vpin/)
- [Kyle's Lambda](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/kyles-lambda/)
- [Order Flow Imbalance (OFI)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/ofi/)

# Sharpe Ratio

> Mean excess return divided by the standard deviation of excess return, annualised by the square root of the number of periods per year. The same definition as the performance calculator on this site.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/sharpe-ratio/

Category: Performance & Risk Metrics. Term ID: `sharpe-ratio`.

## Definition

The Sharpe ratio asks how much excess return a series delivered per unit of volatility. Excess is the periodic return minus a periodic risk-free rate. The rate used here is an annual rate converted by compound interest, (1 + r_f)^(1/P) − 1, not a simple r_f/P. Volatility is the sample standard deviation (divide by n − 1). Annualisation multiplies by sqrt(P). A higher number means more excess return per unit of variability in that sample. It is not a forecast and it is not a certificate of skill.

## Formula

```
r_f,period = (1 + r_f,annual) ^ (1/P) − 1
excess_t   = R_t − r_f,period

Sharpe = mean(excess) / std(excess, ddof=1) · sqrt(P)

P = 252 by default, 242 for China A-shares, 365 for a crypto-style calendar.
std = 0 → the ratio is undefined (returned as NaN).
```

## Conventions that change the number

- The [performance calculator](https://quantcore-labs.com/tools/performance-analytics/) uses this compounding convention, sample standard deviation, and the same sqrt(P) annualisation. The glossary function is written to match it.
- Some published Sharpes subtract r_f/P, or divide by the population standard deviation, or leave the ratio un-annualised. Those are different statistics. Quote P and the risk-free treatment next to the number.
- Downside-only volatility is the [Sortino ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/sortino-ratio/). Active return over tracking error is the [information ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/information-ratio/).

## Pitfalls

- **It is a sample moment.** A short window, or a window that happens to contain one regime, moves the ratio a lot. It does not carry a promise about the next window.
- **Volatility is not the risk you may care about.** Two series with the same Sharpe can have very different [drawdowns](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/max-drawdown/) and tail losses. See also [VaR and expected shortfall](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/var-expected-shortfall/).
- **Illiquid and smoothed returns look better.** A series that only updates occasionally understates standard deviation and overstates Sharpe. The same is true of a backtest that ignores costs.
- **Annualising assumes i.i.d. periods.** Strong autocorrelation makes sqrt(P) the wrong scaling. The function still multiplies by sqrt(P); the assumption is yours to check.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/sharpe-ratio/sharpe-ratio.py

```python
import numpy as np

def sharpe_ratio(returns, rf_annual=0.0, periods=252) -> float:
    """Annualised Sharpe ratio.

    rf_annual is compounded to a per-period rate: (1 + rf_annual) ** (1/periods) - 1.
    Volatility is the sample standard deviation of excess returns. Zero volatility
    returns NaN. This matches /tools/performance-analytics/.
    """
    r = np.asarray(returns, dtype=float)
    r = r[np.isfinite(r)]
    if r.size < 2:
        raise ValueError("need at least two finite returns")
    if periods <= 0:
        raise ValueError("periods must be positive")
    rf = (1.0 + rf_annual) ** (1.0 / periods) - 1.0
    excess = r - rf
    sd = float(excess.std(ddof=1))
    if sd == 0.0:
        return float("nan")
    return float(excess.mean() / sd * np.sqrt(periods))
```

## FAQ

**Why compound the risk-free rate instead of dividing by 252?**

An annual rate of 2 percent is not 2/252 per day under compound interest. The per-period rate that compounds back to 2 percent is (1.02)^(1/252) − 1, which is slightly less than 2/252. The difference is small at low rates and is the convention the performance calculator on this site uses.

**Is a Sharpe ratio of 1 good?**

It means the sample's mean excess return equalled its annualised volatility. Whether that is attractive depends on the sample, the costs that were left out, and the drawdowns. The ratio is not a threshold for taking a position.

## Related

- [Sortino Ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/sortino-ratio/)
- [Information Ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/information-ratio/)
- [Maximum Drawdown](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/max-drawdown/)
- [Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/var-expected-shortfall/)

# Sortino Ratio

> Mean return above a minimum acceptable return, divided by downside deviation and annualised. Upside variation does not enter the denominator.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/sortino-ratio/

Category: Performance & Risk Metrics. Term ID: `sortino-ratio`.

## Definition

The Sortino ratio replaces the Sharpe denominator with downside deviation: the root-mean-square of returns that fall short of a target, with shortfalls of zero on periods that meet the target still included in the average. The target used here is an annual minimum acceptable return, converted to a per-period rate the same way the risk-free rate is converted for the Sharpe ratio. The result is annualised by sqrt(P). It penalises missing the target. It does not penalise beating it.

## Formula

```
MAR_period = (1 + MAR_annual) ^ (1/P) − 1
d_t = min(R_t − MAR_period, 0)
DD  = sqrt( mean(d_t²) )                 average over every period, not only the negative ones

Sortino = (mean(R) − MAR_period) / DD · sqrt(P)

DD = 0 → undefined (NaN). Using only the negative periods in the mean would be a different statistic.
```

## Why the denominator ignores upside

- Two strategies can share a volatility and a [Sharpe ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/sharpe-ratio/) while one of them makes its volatility on the upside. Sortino treats those as different.
- The target is not automatically the risk-free rate. It is whatever minimum acceptable return you pass in. Zero means "negative periodic returns count against the strategy".
- The [performance calculator](https://quantcore-labs.com/tools/performance-analytics/) uses this downside definition (root-mean-square over all periods) and the same annualisation.

## Pitfalls

- **A sample with no down period is undefined, not infinite.** The function returns NaN. Reporting a huge Sortino from a handful of up days is a presentation choice the code refuses.
- **The mean in the square root is over n, not n − 1.** That matches the calculator. Mixing it with a sample-standard-deviation downside changes the number.
- **It still does not see path.** A slow grind below the target and a crash with the same squared shortfalls can share a Sortino. Look at [maximum drawdown](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/max-drawdown/) as well.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/sortino-ratio/sortino-ratio.py

```python
import numpy as np

def sortino_ratio(returns, mar_annual=0.0, periods=252) -> float:
    """Annualised Sortino ratio.

    Downside deviation is the root-mean-square of min(r - MAR, 0) over all
    periods. MAR is an annual rate, compounded to a per-period rate.
    No downside variation returns NaN. Matches /tools/performance-analytics/.
    """
    r = np.asarray(returns, dtype=float)
    r = r[np.isfinite(r)]
    if r.size < 2:
        raise ValueError("need at least two finite returns")
    if periods <= 0:
        raise ValueError("periods must be positive")
    mar = (1.0 + mar_annual) ** (1.0 / periods) - 1.0
    downside = float(np.sqrt(np.mean(np.minimum(r - mar, 0.0) ** 2)))
    if downside == 0.0:
        return float("nan")
    return float((r.mean() - mar) / downside * np.sqrt(periods))
```

## FAQ

**Why average the squared shortfalls over periods that were not shortfalls?**

Those periods contribute a zero, so they dilute the root-mean-square. Dropping them would divide by the number of bad periods only and would make a rare crash look like a small downside. The version that keeps the zeros is the one the performance calculator uses.

**Should the target be the risk-free rate?**

Only if that is the return you have decided is the minimum you care about. The parameter is a minimum acceptable return, not a funding rate. Leaving it at zero scores any negative periodic return as downside.

## Related

- [Sharpe Ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/sharpe-ratio/)
- [Maximum Drawdown](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/max-drawdown/)
- [Calmar Ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/calmar-ratio/)

# Information Ratio

> Mean active return versus a benchmark, divided by the tracking error of that active return, and annualised. It scores how large and how steady the gap versus the benchmark was.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/information-ratio/

Category: Performance & Risk Metrics. Term ID: `information-ratio`.

## Definition

Active return is the portfolio's periodic return minus the benchmark's periodic return over the same periods. The information ratio is the mean of that difference divided by its sample standard deviation, multiplied by sqrt(P). It is the Sharpe ratio of the active returns, with the benchmark playing the role of the risk-free asset and no extra cash rate. A positive ratio means the portfolio's sample average was above the benchmark. It does not say the average will stay there.

## Formula

```
a_t = R_port,t − R_bench,t
IR  = mean(a) / std(a, ddof=1) · sqrt(P)

Tracking error is the denominator before dividing into the mean: TE = std(a) · sqrt(P).
IR = mean(a) · sqrt(P) / TE, with TE in annualised units.
std(a) = 0 → NaN (the portfolio matched the benchmark exactly in-sample).
```

## Relation to other ratios

- [Tracking error](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/tracking-error/) is the annualised standard deviation alone. The information ratio puts the mean active return on top of it.
- The [information coefficient](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/information-coefficient/) is a cross-sectional correlation between a signal and later returns, not this time-series ratio. Grinold's approximation IR ≈ IC · sqrt(breadth) is a model that links them, not an identity in the data.
- A [Sharpe ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/sharpe-ratio/) uses excess return over cash. An information ratio uses excess return over the benchmark you were hired to beat, or chose to compare with.

## Pitfalls

- **The benchmark has to be the one that was investable on that timing.** Comparing a close-to-close portfolio with a benchmark that includes a return the portfolio could not have earned inflates the ratio.
- **Alignment.** Missing dates, dividends in one series only, or a different currency, all land in the active return. The function subtracts the two arrays as given.
- **A high IR on a tiny active risk** can be a few basis points of average difference and a tracking error that is mostly noise. Report the tracking error beside the ratio.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/information-ratio/information-ratio.py

```python
import numpy as np

def information_ratio(port, bench, periods=252) -> float:
    """Annualised information ratio of port minus bench.

    Sample standard deviation. Identical series return NaN.
    """
    active = np.asarray(port, dtype=float) - np.asarray(bench, dtype=float)
    if active.ndim != 1 or active.size < 2 or not np.all(np.isfinite(active)):
        raise ValueError("need at least two finite paired returns")
    if periods <= 0:
        raise ValueError("periods must be positive")
    sd = float(active.std(ddof=1))
    if sd == 0.0:
        return float("nan")
    return float(active.mean() / sd * np.sqrt(periods))
```

## FAQ

**How is this different from the information coefficient?**

The information coefficient correlates a cross-section of forecasts with a cross-section of outcomes on one date. The information ratio divides a time series of active returns by their standard deviation. Similar names, different objects.

**Should the active return include fees?**

If the question is what the investor kept versus the benchmark, yes. If the question is whether the holdings differed from the benchmark before costs, no. The function uses the two return series you pass in, so the choice of fees happens before the call.

## Related

- [Tracking Error](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/tracking-error/)
- [Sharpe Ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/sharpe-ratio/)
- [Information Coefficient (IC)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/information-coefficient/)
- [Beta](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/beta/)

# Tracking Error

> The annualised sample standard deviation of portfolio return minus benchmark return. It measures how far the two series wandered from each other, not whether one ended ahead.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/tracking-error/

Category: Performance & Risk Metrics. Term ID: `tracking-error`.

## Definition

Tracking error is the volatility of active returns. A portfolio that beats its benchmark by exactly one basis point every period has a positive average active return and a tracking error of zero. A portfolio that oscillates around the benchmark has tracking error and, possibly, a zero average. The implementation is the sample standard deviation of the paired difference, times sqrt(P).

## Formula

```
a_t = R_port,t − R_bench,t
TE  = std(a, ddof=1) · sqrt(P)

P defaults to 252. Reported as a decimal (0.02 means 2 percent annualised), not in basis points.
The information ratio is mean(a) / std(a) · sqrt(P), so IR = annualised mean active return / TE.
```

## Where it shows up

- Index tracking and closet indexing. A mandate that says "stay within 2 percent tracking error" is a constraint on this number, usually estimated on an ex-ante covariance as well as measured ex post. This function is the ex-post measurement.
- Next to the [information ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/information-ratio/), which is undefined when tracking error is zero.
- [Beta](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/beta/) is a different summary of the same pair of series: a slope, not the volatility of the residual gap. Two portfolios can share a beta and have very different tracking errors.

## Pitfalls

- **Ex post is not ex ante.** The standard deviation of realised active returns is not the tracking error a covariance model would predict for the current holdings.
- **Annualisation.** Multiplying a daily active-return standard deviation by sqrt(252) assumes uncorrelated active returns. A persistent active bet (a permanent sector tilt) has a tracking error that does not scale that way if you change the sampling interval without care. Be consistent about P.
- **Levels versus returns.** Tracking error is defined on returns. A price spread between an ETF and its basket is a different measurement.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/tracking-error/tracking-error.py

```python
import numpy as np

def tracking_error(port, bench, periods=252) -> float:
    """Annualised sample standard deviation of port minus bench."""
    active = np.asarray(port, dtype=float) - np.asarray(bench, dtype=float)
    if active.ndim != 1 or active.size < 2 or not np.all(np.isfinite(active)):
        raise ValueError("need at least two finite paired returns")
    if periods <= 0:
        raise ValueError("periods must be positive")
    return float(active.std(ddof=1) * np.sqrt(periods))
```

## FAQ

**Can tracking error be zero while the portfolio differs from the benchmark?**

Yes, if the difference in returns is constant. Standard deviation does not see the mean. A constant lag of one basis point per day is a large cumulative gap and a zero tracking error.

**Is tracking error the same as active risk?**

In mandate language, active risk usually means this volatility of active returns, sometimes the ex-ante forecast of it. Quote whether the number is realised or predicted. This function is realised.

## Related

- [Information Ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/information-ratio/)
- [Beta](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/beta/)
- [Sharpe Ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/sharpe-ratio/)

# Maximum Drawdown

> The most negative peak-to-trough decline of an equity curve. A 25 percent decline is returned as −0.25, not as 0.25.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/max-drawdown/

Category: Performance & Risk Metrics. Term ID: `max-drawdown`.

## Definition

Drawdown at each point is the equity divided by the highest equity seen so far, minus one. The maximum drawdown is the smallest of those numbers (the deepest loss from a peak). It is path dependent: the order of returns matters, not only their mean and variance. The function expects a positive equity curve, not a return series.

## Formula

```
DD_t = E_t / max_{s ≤ t} E_s − 1
MDD  = min_t DD_t

MDD ≤ 0. MDD = 0 means the equity curve never fell below a peak it had already set.
Recovery and the length of the drawdown are not part of this number.
```

## Using it next to a return ratio

- Sharpe and Sortino compress the path into moments. Maximum drawdown keeps one fact about the path: the worst decline from a high-water mark. Report both.
- The [performance calculator](https://quantcore-labs.com/tools/performance-analytics/) uses this definition and also reports how long the longest drawdown lasted. Duration is not in the function on this page.
- [Calmar](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/calmar-ratio/) divides annualised growth by the absolute value of this number.

## Pitfalls

- **Sign.** The function returns a non-positive fraction. Taking abs is the caller's job when a report wants "25 percent drawdown" as a positive phrase. Calmar does that internally.
- **Equity, not returns.** Passing returns produces a meaningless ratio of small numbers. Compound the returns to equity first. The first point is a peak by definition, so a curve that falls immediately draws down from the starting level.
- **Sample length.** A longer window can only make the maximum worse or leave it unchanged, if it contains the shorter window. Comparing a one-year MDD with a ten-year MDD as if they were the same statistic favours the short window.
- **Mark-to-market frequency.** Daily equity and monthly equity do not share a maximum drawdown. Intra-month peaks are invisible on a monthly curve.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/max-drawdown/max-drawdown.py

```python
import numpy as np

def max_drawdown(equity) -> float:
    """Most negative peak-to-trough decline of a positive equity curve.

    Returns a fraction in [-1, 0]. A 25% decline is -0.25.
    """
    equity = np.asarray(equity, dtype=float)
    if equity.size == 0 or not np.all(np.isfinite(equity)) or np.any(equity <= 0):
        raise ValueError("equity must be non-empty, finite and positive")
    peak = np.maximum.accumulate(equity)
    return float((equity / peak - 1.0).min())
```

## FAQ

**Does the maximum drawdown say when it happened?**

No. It is a single fraction. The performance calculator on this site also reports the peak and trough dates and the longest time spent below a peak. Those need the whole drawdown path, not only its minimum.

**What if the curve ends at its low?**

The unrecovered decline is included. Maximum drawdown does not require the equity to have made a new high afterwards. A strategy that fell 40 percent and never recovered has a maximum drawdown of at least 40 percent.

## Related

- [Calmar Ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/calmar-ratio/)
- [Sharpe Ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/sharpe-ratio/)
- [Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/var-expected-shortfall/)

---

# Calmar Ratio

> Compound annual growth of an equity curve divided by the absolute value of its maximum drawdown. This implementation uses the whole sample, not a trailing 36-month window.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/calmar-ratio/

Category: Performance & Risk Metrics. Term ID: `calmar-ratio`.

## Definition

Calmar divides a growth rate by the worst peak-to-trough loss over the window you care about. Here the growth rate is the compound annual growth that takes the first equity point to the last, using P periods per year, and the loss is the maximum drawdown of the same points. A curve that never falls has an undefined Calmar, returned as NaN, rather than an infinite one. The original published ratio used a trailing three-year window. Using the whole sample is what the performance calculator on this site does, and it will not match a 36-month Calmar when the sample is a different length.

## Formula

```
n = number of returns = (number of equity points) − 1
CAGR = (E_last / E_first) ^ (P / n) − 1
MDD  = min_t (E_t / max_{s≤t} E_s − 1)          MDD ≤ 0

Calmar = CAGR / |MDD|     if MDD < 0, else undefined

P defaults to 252. The same equity series should be used for the numerator and the denominator.
```

## Reading it

- A Calmar of 0.5 means the compound annual growth was half the size of the worst decline, on this sample and this annualisation. It is not a forecast of either input.
- The pieces are on their own pages: growth uses the same exponent as the [performance calculator](https://quantcore-labs.com/tools/performance-analytics/), and the denominator is [maximum drawdown](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/max-drawdown/).
- Sharpe uses a typical deviation. Calmar uses a single worst episode. One deep drawdown dominates it, which is the point of the ratio and also its instability.

## Pitfalls

- **Window.** Young (1991) described a three-year lookback. A ten-year Calmar and a three-year Calmar of the same fund are different statistics. This function uses every point you pass.
- **Start and end dates are part of the answer.** CAGR depends on the first and last equity. MDD depends on the path between them. Dropping a crash from the sample changes the denominator; ending on a peak changes the numerator.
- **Frequency.** P has to match the spacing of the equity points. Passing daily equity with P = 12 treats a year of days as twelve periods.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/calmar-ratio/calmar-ratio.py

```python
import numpy as np

def calmar_ratio(equity, periods=252) -> float:
    """CAGR / |maximum drawdown| over the whole sample.

    CAGR uses (E_last / E_first) ** (periods / n_returns) - 1.
    A curve with no drawdown returns NaN. Matches the full-sample convention
    of /tools/performance-analytics/, not a trailing 36-month window.
    """
    equity = np.asarray(equity, dtype=float)
    if equity.size < 2 or not np.all(np.isfinite(equity)) or np.any(equity <= 0):
        raise ValueError("need at least two positive finite equity points")
    if periods <= 0:
        raise ValueError("periods must be positive")
    n = equity.size - 1
    cagr = (equity[-1] / equity[0]) ** (periods / n) - 1.0
    mdd = float((equity / np.maximum.accumulate(equity) - 1.0).min())
    if mdd == 0.0:
        return float("nan")
    return float(cagr / abs(mdd))
```

## FAQ

**Why not use a 36-month window?**

The original Calmar ratio did. This site's performance calculator divides full-sample CAGR by full-sample maximum drawdown, and the glossary function matches that so the two do not disagree. For a 36-month figure, pass only those points.

**What does NaN mean here?**

The equity curve made no new low relative to a peak, so the denominator would be zero. That includes a curve that only rises. It is not an infinite reward-to-risk ratio.

## Related

- [Maximum Drawdown](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/max-drawdown/)
- [Sharpe Ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/sharpe-ratio/)
- [Sortino Ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/sortino-ratio/)

---

# Kelly Criterion

> The bet size that maximises expected logarithmic growth. For a binary bet it is an exact fraction of wealth. For a continuous return it is approximately mean over variance. It is a sizing formula, not advice to use it.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/kelly-criterion/

Category: Position Sizing. Term ID: `kelly-criterion`.

## Definition

A log-utility investor who can repeat the same bet wants the fraction of wealth that maximises the expected log of wealth after the bet. For a binary outcome that pays net odds b with probability p, that fraction is p − (1 − p) / b. For a continuous excess return with mean μ and variance σ², the corresponding unconstrained fraction is approximately μ / σ² when the higher moments are ignored. Estimated μ and σ² are noisy, and the full fraction is aggressive when the estimate is wrong, so practitioners who use the idea often scale it down. Nothing on this page says that an investor should.

## Formula

```
Binary bet, win probability p, net odds b (win b for each 1 staked):
  f* = p − (1 − p) / b = (b p − (1 − p)) / b

Continuous approximation, excess mean μ and variance σ² over the same horizon:
  f* ≈ μ / σ²

f* < 0 means the edge is negative: the formula says stake nothing on that side.
f* > 1 means the approximation wants leverage. The binary formula assumes you cannot stake more than wealth if you cap it; this function does not cap.
```

## What the two formulas assume

- The binary formula is exact for one repeated i.i.d. bet with known p and b, and for an objective that only cares about expected log wealth. Change the objective and the fraction changes.
- The continuous formula is a small-bet or diffusion approximation. It ignores skew and the chance of a loss large enough to make the log argument non-positive. A return distribution with a fat left tail is exactly where that matters.
- Volatility in the denominator is the same object as in the [Sharpe ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/sharpe-ratio/), but the Kelly fraction is not a Sharpe ratio. Sharpe divides by standard deviation and annualises. Kelly divides by variance and is a weight.

## Pitfalls

- **The inputs are estimates.** Full Kelly computed from a sample mean is famous for suggesting large weights that were an artefact of the sample. A fraction of the estimate (half Kelly, quarter Kelly) is a common ad-hoc shrink. This code does not apply one.
- **No drawdown constraint.** Log growth can coexist with deep [drawdowns](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/max-drawdown/). The formula does not know your limit.
- **Odds b are net odds.** Even money is b = 1, not 2. Passing the decimal payout instead of the net profit doubles-counts the stake and shrinks f*.
- **Not a recommendation.** The function returns a number from an objective. It does not say the bet is worth making.

## Python reference implementation

Requires standard library. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/kelly-criterion/kelly-criterion.py

```python
def kelly_fraction(p, b) -> float:
    """Fraction of wealth for a binary bet. p = win probability, b = net odds.

    f* = p - (1 - p) / b. Does not cap at 0 or 1. Not a recommendation to bet.
    """
    p, b = float(p), float(b)
    if not 0.0 <= p <= 1.0:
        raise ValueError("p must be in [0, 1]")
    if b <= 0:
        raise ValueError("b, the net odds, must be positive")
    return p - (1.0 - p) / b

def kelly_continuous(mu, variance) -> float:
    """Approximate Kelly fraction mu / variance for a continuous excess return.

    Ignores higher moments. Not a position-sizing recommendation.
    """
    mu, variance = float(mu), float(variance)
    if variance <= 0:
        raise ValueError("variance must be positive")
    return mu / variance
```

## FAQ

**Why do people use half Kelly?**

Because p, b, μ and σ² plugged into the formula are estimates, and the expected log growth falls off slowly just below the optimum and steeply above it. Betting less than the estimated full fraction gives up a little growth on the estimated edge and hurts less when the edge was overstated. Half is a convention, not a theorem, and this page does not apply it.

**What does a negative fraction mean?**

For the binary bet, the probability and the odds do not compensate each other: expected log wealth is higher at a stake of zero than at a long stake. It is not an instruction to take the other side unless that side is a bet you can actually price with its own p and b.

## Related

- [Sharpe Ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/sharpe-ratio/)
- [Maximum Drawdown](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/max-drawdown/)

# Beta

> The OLS slope of an asset's returns on a market's returns: covariance divided by the market's variance. It is the CAPM coefficient on the sample you pass in, not a forecast.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/beta/

Category: Portfolio & Factor Models. Term ID: `beta`.

## Definition

Beta measures how much an asset's return tended to move with the market return in a sample. It is Cov(R_i, R_m) / Var(R_m), which is also the slope of a regression of the asset on the market with an intercept. A beta of 1 means the asset moved one-for-one with the market on average, after the intercept absorbed the mean difference. It says nothing, by itself, about residual risk or about whether the sample will repeat.

## Formula

```
β = Cov(R_i, R_m) / Var(R_m)

Sample covariance and variance, ddof = 1 (the OLS slope).
The intercept α = mean(R_i) − β · mean(R_m) is not returned.
Var(R_m) = 0 → undefined; the function raises.

CAPM uses a beta against the market excess return. This function uses the two series you pass. If they are excess returns, β is the CAPM slope; if they are raw returns, it is a raw-return slope.
```

## What it is not

- It is not correlation. Correlation divides by both standard deviations and lies in [−1, 1]. Beta is in the units of "asset return per unit of market return" and can sit far outside that interval.
- It is not [tracking error](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/tracking-error/). Tracking error is the volatility of the gap. Beta is the slope. An index fund should have a beta near 1 and a small tracking error; a leveraged index fund can have a beta near 2 and still a small residual.
- It is not the [Sharpe ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/sharpe-ratio/). Sharpe has no benchmark series other than cash.

## Pitfalls

- **Unstable in short samples.** A 60-day beta and a five-year beta of the same name often disagree. The function does not shrink toward 1. If you want a shrunk beta, do it after the call and say so.
- **The market series is the definition of the beta.** A national equity index, a futures excess return and a global market portfolio produce three different numbers. The symbol β does not record which one you used.
- **Changing composition.** Beta of a portfolio computed from the portfolio's past returns describes the portfolio as it was, including positions it no longer holds.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/beta/beta.py

```python
import numpy as np

def beta(asset, market) -> float:
    """OLS slope Cov(asset, market) / Var(market), sample moments (ddof=1)."""
    a = np.asarray(asset, dtype=float)
    m = np.asarray(market, dtype=float)
    if a.shape != m.shape or a.ndim != 1 or a.size < 2:
        raise ValueError("need at least two aligned returns")
    if not np.all(np.isfinite(a)) or not np.all(np.isfinite(m)):
        raise ValueError("returns must be finite")
    var_m = float(np.var(m, ddof=1))
    if var_m <= 0:
        raise ValueError("market variance is zero")
    cov = float(np.cov(a, m, ddof=1)[0, 1])
    return cov / var_m
```

## FAQ

**Does beta include an intercept?**

The slope from Cov/Var is exactly the OLS slope when an intercept is allowed. The intercept is the average return not explained by the market in that sample. This function returns only the slope.

**Why did I get a beta far from my broker's beta?**

The window, the frequency, the market series and whether returns are excess or raw all change the slope. Two betas are comparable when those choices match. This function documents none of them except the arithmetic, which is sample covariance over sample variance.

## Related

- [Tracking Error](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/tracking-error/)
- [Information Ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/information-ratio/)
- [Sharpe Ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/sharpe-ratio/)

# Realized Volatility

> The square root of the sum of squared log returns inside one window, optionally scaled to a year. For a single day of intraday prices, multiplying by 252 annualises that day's realized variance. Do not do that to a stack of many days.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/realized-volatility/

Category: Volatility Modeling. Term ID: `realized-volatility`.

## Definition

Realized variance over a window is the sum of squared logarithmic returns of the prices inside it. Realized volatility is its square root. Under a diffusion with no jumps, that sum estimates the integrated variance of the window, and finer sampling makes the estimate tighter until microstructure noise dominates. The function annualises by multiplying the sum by a periods-per-year factor before the square root. That factor is correct when the sum is one period's variance (one day, if the factor is 252). Applied to a year of already-daily returns it multiplies a yearly total by 252 and overstates volatility by about sqrt(252).

## Formula

```
r_i = ln(P_i / P_{i−1})
RV  = sqrt( (Σ_i r_i²) · P )

P = periods per year used to annualise THIS window.
One day of intraday returns → P = 252 (or 242) gives an annualised number from that day.
A window you do not want to annualise → P = 1, which returns sqrt(Σ r_i²).

The sum of squares, not the square of the sum. Signs of returns do not matter.
```

## What the window is

- Pass the prices of one period. A session of one-minute prices in, an annualised volatility for that session out, if you set the factor to the number of sessions in a year.
- To describe a year, compute each day's sum of squares and then average the daily realized variances, and only then scale. This function does not do that average. It scales whatever sum you hand it.
- Close-to-close volatility is the ordinary standard deviation of daily log returns, a different estimator. Range estimators such as [Parkinson](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/parkinson-volatility/) use high and low. A conditional model is [GARCH](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/garch/).

## Pitfalls

- **Annualisation is the easy mistake.** Σ r² over 252 daily returns is already a year of variance. Multiplying by another 252 is wrong. Use P = 1 for a pre-aggregated sum you do not want scaled.
- **Microstructure.** Bid-ask bounce biases the sum of squares up as the sampling gets finer. One-second returns on a wide spread mostly measure the spread.
- **Jumps and overnight.** A close-to-open jump is one large r_i if you include it, and is invisible if you only pass the cash session. Neither choice is free.
- **Zeros and negative prices.** Log returns require positive prices. The function rejects the rest.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/realized-volatility/realized-volatility.py

```python
import numpy as np

def realized_vol(prices, periods_per_year=252) -> float:
    """Square root of summed squared log returns, scaled by periods_per_year.

    periods_per_year annualises a SINGLE window. Use 1 to return the
    un-annualised sqrt(sum of squares). Prices must be positive.
    """
    px = np.asarray(prices, dtype=float)
    if px.size < 2 or not np.all(np.isfinite(px)) or np.any(px <= 0):
        raise ValueError("need at least two positive finite prices")
    if periods_per_year <= 0:
        raise ValueError("periods_per_year must be positive")
    r = np.diff(np.log(px))
    return float(np.sqrt(np.sum(r * r) * periods_per_year))
```

## FAQ

**How do I annualise a year of daily realized variances?**

Average the daily sums of squared intraday returns first (that average estimates average daily variance), then multiply by the number of sessions in a year and take the square root. Passing every intraday price of the year into this function with periods_per_year=252 multiplies a year of variance by 252.

**Why log returns?**

Squared log returns add up to integrated variance for a diffusion. Squared simple returns are close when the moves are small and are a different estimator when they are not. The function uses logs.

## Related

- [Parkinson Volatility](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/parkinson-volatility/)
- [GARCH(1,1)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/garch/)
- [Implied Volatility](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/implied-volatility/)

# Parkinson Volatility

> A volatility estimator that uses each period's high and low instead of the close-to-close move. Under a driftless Brownian motion it is more efficient than the close-to-close estimator. With drift, jumps or a close that is not the whole story, that efficiency result does not apply.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/parkinson-volatility/

Category: Volatility Modeling. Term ID: `parkinson-volatility`.

## Definition

Parkinson (1980) replaces the squared close-to-close return with the squared log range. The scaling 1 / (4 ln 2) makes the average of those squared ranges an estimate of the variance per period, for a Brownian motion with no drift. Multiplying by the number of periods in a year and taking the square root annualises it. The estimator never sees the open or the close. A day that gaps and then trades in a narrow range looks quiet.

## Formula

```
σ²_period = (1 / (4 N ln 2)) · Σ_{t=1..N} (ln(H_t / L_t))²
σ_annual  = σ_period · sqrt(P)

H_t ≥ L_t > 0.  N is the number of ranges you pass.
4 ln 2 ≈ 2.7726, so a day whose high is about 1.7% above its low
(ln(H/L) ≈ 0.0166, squared ≈ 2.77e-4) contributes about 1e-4 of daily variance
before annualisation, i.e. 1 percent daily, before the average.

P defaults to 252 and scales the mean daily variance, which is the right
shape when each row is one session.
```

## Why a range

- The high and the low summarise the whole path, not only the two endpoints. For a driftless Brownian motion the range estimator has a lower variance than the close-to-close estimator on the same number of days.
- It is a natural check on [realized volatility](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/realized-volatility/) when you have bars but not a full trade tape: daily high and low are enough.
- It is still a historical number. An option-implied number is [implied volatility](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/implied-volatility/), and a recursive filter is [GARCH](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/garch/).

## Pitfalls

- **Drift.** A strong trend widens the range for a reason other than diffusion variance. Parkinson is derived at zero drift. Rogers-Satchell and Yang-Zhang exist because of that; this page does not implement them.
- **Overnight gaps.** If high and low are the cash-session extrema, the gap from yesterday's close is invisible. The estimator then misses a piece of the day's variance that a close-to-close number includes.
- **Bad prints.** One erroneous high dominates a squared range. The average does not trim it.
- **Do not feed intraday bars and also multiply by 252** unless each row is one session. The function annualises the mean of the rows you pass.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/parkinson-volatility/parkinson-volatility.py

```python
import numpy as np

def parkinson_vol(high, low, periods=252) -> float:
    """Annualised Parkinson volatility from high and low arrays.

    Each pair is one period. `periods` is how many such periods make a year.
    Requires 0 < low <= high.
    """
    h = np.asarray(high, dtype=float)
    lo = np.asarray(low, dtype=float)
    if h.shape != lo.shape or h.ndim != 1 or h.size == 0:
        raise ValueError("high and low must be non-empty and aligned")
    if not np.all(np.isfinite(h)) or not np.all(np.isfinite(lo)):
        raise ValueError("high and low must be finite")
    if np.any(lo <= 0) or np.any(h < lo):
        raise ValueError("require 0 < low <= high")
    if periods <= 0:
        raise ValueError("periods must be positive")
    x = np.log(h / lo)
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean(x * x) / (4.0 * np.log(2.0)) * periods))
```

## FAQ

**Why is the divisor 4 ln 2?**

It is the expected value of the squared log range of a standard Brownian motion over one unit of time. Dividing by it converts an average squared range into a variance estimate. The derivation assumes no drift and no jumps.

**Is Parkinson always better than close-to-close?**

No. It is more efficient in the zero-drift diffusion it was derived for. A large overnight gap, a trading halt, or a bad high print can make it worse than a close-to-close estimator that at least uses the official closes.

## Related

- [Realized Volatility](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/realized-volatility/)
- [GARCH(1,1)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/garch/)
- [Implied Volatility](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/implied-volatility/)

# GARCH(1,1)

> A conditional variance that is a constant plus a weight on yesterday's squared shock plus a weight on yesterday's variance. This page filters a series with given parameters. It does not estimate them.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/garch/

Category: Volatility Modeling. Term ID: `garch`.

## Definition

GARCH(1,1), Bollerslev (1986), says today's variance depends on a long-run piece, on how large yesterday's surprise was, and on yesterday's variance. Clusters of large moves follow because a large shock raises the next variance, which keeps later variances high until the β term decays. The function below runs that recursion. ω, α and β are inputs. Fitting them by maximum likelihood is a numerical problem this page does not solve. The variance at step 0 is the first squared return, so the filter does not use later data to start itself.

## Formula

```
σ²_t = ω + α ε²_{t−1} + β σ²_{t−1}

σ²_0 = ε_0²          (a one-point start; not the sample variance of the whole series)
Unconditional variance, when α ≥ 0, β ≥ 0 and α + β < 1:
  σ²_∞ = ω / (1 − α − β)

α + β is the persistence. α + β ≥ 1 means there is no finite unconditional variance.
The filter still runs. Half-life of a shock to variance is about ln(2) / −ln(α+β) periods when α+β < 1.

EWMA is the case ω = 0, α + β = 1, with α = 1−λ and β = λ. See the Numba EWMA page.
```

## Filter versus estimate

- Given parameters, the recursion is a one-pass filter. That is what `garch11_variance` does, and what the tests check.
- The parameters themselves are usually estimated by maximising a Gaussian or Student-t likelihood. Different likelihoods, different estimates. Publishing a 20-line fitter here would hide that choice.
- Compare the path with [realized volatility](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/realized-volatility/) (a sum of squares, no parameters) and with [EWMA](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/numba-ewma-volatility/) (persistence fixed at 1).

## Pitfalls

- **The shock is the return only if the mean is zero.** The recursion treats the series you pass as ε. If you meant a demeaned residual, demean first. A large mean inside ε² looks like volatility.
- **Starting value.** ε_0² can be a wild first day. An alternative is the unconditional variance, which depends on the parameters and, if those were fit on this same sample, uses the whole sample. This filter does not do that.
- **α + β close to 1** makes the unconditional variance huge and the filter slow to forget. Integrated GARCH (α + β = 1) never forgets a shock in the level of variance.
- **No leverage term.** Plain GARCH treats an up move and a down move of the same size identically. GJR and EGARCH exist because equity returns usually do not.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/garch/garch.py

```python
import numpy as np

def garch11_variance(returns, omega, alpha, beta):
    """GARCH(1,1) variance path. Parameters are inputs, not estimates.

    var[0] = returns[0] ** 2. Later terms use the previous return and the
    previous variance only. omega, alpha, beta must be non-negative.
    """
    r = np.asarray(returns, dtype=float)
    if r.ndim != 1 or not np.all(np.isfinite(r)):
        raise ValueError("returns must be a finite 1-d array")
    if omega < 0 or alpha < 0 or beta < 0:
        raise ValueError("omega, alpha and beta must be non-negative")
    var = np.empty(r.shape, dtype=float)
    if r.size == 0:
        return var
    var[0] = r[0] * r[0]
    for t in range(1, r.size):
        var[t] = omega + alpha * r[t - 1] * r[t - 1] + beta * var[t - 1]
    return var

def garch11_unconditional(omega, alpha, beta) -> float:
    """ω / (1 − α − β). Inf when α + β ≥ 1."""
    if omega < 0 or alpha < 0 or beta < 0:
        raise ValueError("omega, alpha and beta must be non-negative")
    if alpha + beta >= 1.0:
        return float("inf")
    return float(omega / (1.0 - alpha - beta))
```

## FAQ

**Why not fit the parameters on this page?**

A Gaussian likelihood, a Student-t likelihood and a robust estimator do not return the same (ω, α, β), and the optimiser needs constraints so that variances stay positive. The recursion itself is the part that can be checked exactly. Bring parameters from a fit you trust.

**Is the variance at t allowed to use the return at t?**

Not in this filter. σ²_t is the variance assigned before ε_t is treated as realised, which is what you want if the next step is to standardise ε_t by σ_t. The update that includes ε_t² lands in σ²_{t+1}.

- [Realized Volatility](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/realized-volatility/)
- [Parkinson Volatility](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/parkinson-volatility/)

# Implied Volatility

> The volatility that makes a Black-Scholes-Merton price match an observed option premium. It is solved numerically. There is no closed form for the call price inverted in volatility.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/implied-volatility/

Category: Options & Derivatives. Term ID: `implied-volatility`.

## Definition

Implied volatility is defined by an equation, not by a formula you can rearrange. Given a market premium, a spot, a strike, a time to expiry, a rate and a dividend yield, it is the σ that sets the Black-Scholes-Merton price equal to that premium. This page solves it with Brent's method on a bracket. The same inversion, across strikes and expiries, is what the smile tool on this site plots. A single number always belongs to one contract and one set of inputs.

## Formula

```
C_BSM(S, K, T, r, q, σ_imp) = C_market

d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r − q + σ²/2) T] / (σ √T)
d2 = d1 − σ √T
C  = S e^{−qT} N(d1) − K e^{−rT} N(d2)

No-arbitrage range for a European call, before the solve:
  max(S e^{−qT} − K e^{−rT}, 0) ≤ C ≤ S e^{−qT}
A premium outside that range has no real implied volatility.
```

## Solving it

- The call price increases in σ, so the root is unique when it exists. Brent's method needs a bracket. The code starts at 0.000001 and 5 (500 percent) and widens to 20 if the premium is still above the model at 5.
- A premium that sits on intrinsic value returns 0. A premium outside the no-arbitrage bounds raises, rather than returning a quiet NaN that looks like a failed fit.
- The [implied-volatility smile](https://quantcore-labs.com/tools/iv-smile/) tool solves the same inversion across a grid and fits a slope. One contract's σ_imp is the building block. [Vega](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vega/) is how the price moves when that input moves.

## Pitfalls

- **The model is part of the answer.** A Black-Scholes implied volatility and a Black-76 implied volatility on the same premium are not the same number. This page is Black-Scholes-Merton with a continuous dividend yield q. Set q = 0 for the textbook no-dividend call.
- **European, one expiry, constant inputs.** American early exercise, discrete dividends and a volatility that depends on the strike are all outside the inverter. The smile is exactly the evidence that one σ does not price every strike.
- **Deep, short-dated options.** Vega collapses and many volatilities map to almost the same premium. The root is mathematically there and practically poorly identified. Trust the price residual, not just the σ.

## Python reference implementation

Requires scipy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/implied-volatility/implied-volatility.py

```python
from math import exp, log, sqrt
from scipy.optimize import brentq
from scipy.stats import norm

def bs_call(S, K, T, r, sigma, q=0.0) -> float:
    """Black-Scholes-Merton European call. sigma is a decimal volatility."""
    if S <= 0 or K <= 0 or T <= 0 or sigma <= 0:
        raise ValueError("S, K, T and sigma must be positive")
    sT = sigma * sqrt(T)
    d1 = (log(S / K) + (r - q + 0.5 * sigma * sigma) * T) / sT
    d2 = d1 - sT
    return S * exp(-q * T) * norm.cdf(d1) - K * exp(-r * T) * norm.cdf(d2)

def implied_vol(price, S, K, T, r, q=0.0) -> float:
    """Black-Scholes-Merton implied volatility of a European call premium.

    Returns 0 when the premium is at intrinsic value. Raises when the premium
    is outside the no-arbitrage bounds or the root is above 2000 percent.
    """
    if S <= 0 or K <= 0 or T <= 0:
        raise ValueError("S, K and T must be positive")
    lower = max(S * exp(-q * T) - K * exp(-r * T), 0.0)
    upper = S * exp(-q * T)
    if price < lower - 1e-8 or price > upper + 1e-8:
        raise ValueError("price is outside no-arbitrage bounds")
    if price <= lower + 1e-12:
        return 0.0

    def gap(sigma):
        return bs_call(S, K, T, r, sigma, q) - price

    hi = 5.0
    if gap(hi) < 0:
        hi = 20.0
        if gap(hi) < 0:
            raise ValueError("implied volatility is above 20; check the premium")
    return float(brentq(gap, 1e-6, hi))
```

## FAQ

**Why is there no formula for implied volatility?**

The cumulative normal of d1 and d2 depends on σ in a way that does not invert in closed form. Series approximations exist. A bracketed root find on a monotone function is the straightforward exact method, and it is what this page tests.

**Does a higher implied volatility mean the option is expensive?**

It means the premium is high relative to this model's other inputs. Whether that is expensive depends on the volatility you believe the underlying will actually realise, on the smile, and on costs. The number itself is a restatement of the premium.

## Related

- [Vega](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vega/)
- [Realized Volatility](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/realized-volatility/)
- [GARCH(1,1)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/garch/)
- [Put-Call Parity](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/put-call-parity/)

# Delta

> The derivative of a European option's Black-Scholes-Merton value with respect to the spot. A call delta is e^{−qT} N(d1). A put delta is that quantity minus e^{−qT}.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/delta/

Category: Options & Derivatives. Term ID: `delta`.

## Definition

Delta is how much the model value changes for a small move in the underlying, holding the other inputs fixed. In Black-Scholes-Merton it is a closed form. For a call it lies between 0 and e^{−qT}; for a put it lies between −e^{−qT} and 0. With no dividend yield those bounds are 0 and 1, and −1 and 0. The figure is a model sensitivity. Hedging with it leaves everything the model left out, including jumps and the fact that volatility is not a constant.

## Formula

```
d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r − q + σ²/2) T] / (σ √T)

Δ_call = e^{−qT} N(d1)
Δ_put  = e^{−qT} (N(d1) − 1) = −e^{−qT} N(−d1)

Δ_call − Δ_put = e^{−qT}

q = 0 is the no-dividend textbook case: Δ_call = N(d1), Δ_put = N(d1) − 1.
The on-site calculator uses the same expressions, including q.
```

## How to read the number

- A call delta of 0.50 is not automatically at-the-money once rates or dividends are nonzero. It is the model slope at those inputs. N(d1) equals a half when d1 is zero, which is not the same as S = K.
- Delta of a position is the sum of signed deltas times the multiplier. The function returns the per-unit derivative, not a share count for a book.
- The slope changes as spot moves. That second derivative is [gamma](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/gamma/). The slope also depends on the volatility you typed in, which is where [implied volatility](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/implied-volatility/) enters.

## Pitfalls

- **European Black-Scholes-Merton only.** American puts, barriers and anything path dependent do not have this delta. At expiry the slope becomes a step. The [Greeks calculator](https://quantcore-labs.com/option-greeks-calc/) spells out that limit; this function requires T > 0 and σ > 0 so the formula stays the smooth one.
- **Spot delta versus forward delta.** The derivative here is with respect to spot, and it includes the dividend discount e^{−qT}. A forward delta omits that discount. Mixing them mis-hedges by that factor.
- **A hedge ratio is not a hedge result.** Replacing the option with −Δ shares cancels the first-order spot term in this model, at this instant. Gamma, vega and discrete rebalancing remain.

## Python reference implementation

Requires scipy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/delta/delta.py

```python
from math import exp, log, sqrt
from scipy.stats import norm

def bs_delta(S, K, T, r, sigma, call=True, q=0.0) -> float:
    """Black-Scholes-Merton spot delta. call=False returns the put delta.

    Requires positive S, K, T and sigma. q is a continuous dividend yield.
    """
    if S <= 0 or K <= 0 or T <= 0 or sigma <= 0:
        raise ValueError("S, K, T and sigma must be positive")
    d1 = (log(S / K) + (r - q + 0.5 * sigma * sigma) * T) / (sigma * sqrt(T))
    disc = exp(-q * T)
    return float(disc * norm.cdf(d1) if call else disc * (norm.cdf(d1) - 1.0))
```

## FAQ

**Why is call delta not exactly N(d1)?**

N(d1) is the no-dividend formula. With a continuous yield q the spot delta of a European call is e^{−qT} N(d1). The two agree when q is 0, which is the default of this function.

**Does delta tell me the probability the option finishes in the money?**

No. Under the stock-numeraire measure, N(d1) is a probability related to the share, and N(d2) is the risk-neutral probability that a European call finishes in the money, in this model, with no dividends changing that statement. Neither one is a real-world probability, and neither one is a trading instruction.

## Related

- [Gamma](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/gamma/)
- [Vega](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vega/)
- [Implied Volatility](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/implied-volatility/)
- [Put-Call Parity](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/put-call-parity/)

# Gamma

> The second derivative of a European option's value with respect to the spot, and the derivative of delta. In Black-Scholes-Merton the call and the put of the same strike and expiry have the same gamma.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/gamma/

Category: Options & Derivatives. Term ID: `gamma`.

## Definition

Gamma tells you how fast delta changes as the spot moves. It is largest near the strike and near expiry, where the distribution of finishing in or out of the money is most sensitive to the current spot. Because a European call and put that share strike and expiry differ by a forward (put-call parity), and a forward has no gamma, their gammas are equal. The formula below is that common value.

## Formula

```
Γ = e^{−qT} φ(d1) / (S σ √T)

φ is the standard normal density.
d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r − q + σ²/2) T] / (σ √T)

Same number for the European call and the European put.
Units: change in delta per 1 point of spot. Not a percent.
```

## Why the call and the put match

- [Put-call parity](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/put-call-parity/) says the call minus the put equals a discounted forward. Differentiating twice in S kills the forward and leaves Γ_call = Γ_put.
- Delta does not match. The call delta and the put delta differ by e^{−qT}. See [delta](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/delta/).
- The [Greeks calculator](https://quantcore-labs.com/option-greeks-calc/) reports this gamma for both sides.

## Pitfalls

- **It blows up as expiry approaches** for an option sitting on the strike, because of the √T in the denominator, and it goes to 0 for an option far from the strike. A gamma number with no spot, strike and expiry attached is not interpretable.
- **P&L is not gamma times the move.** The second-order Taylor term is ½ Γ (ΔS)², and it is a model term. Realised moves, hedges and vega P&L are all still there.
- **Spot gamma.** As with delta, this differentiates with respect to spot and includes e^{−qT}. Divide by that discount if you wanted a forward gamma and you meant to.

## Python reference implementation

Requires scipy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/gamma/gamma.py

```python
from math import exp, log, sqrt
from scipy.stats import norm

def bs_gamma(S, K, T, r, sigma, q=0.0) -> float:
    """Black-Scholes-Merton gamma. Identical for the European call and put."""
    if S <= 0 or K <= 0 or T <= 0 or sigma <= 0:
        raise ValueError("S, K, T and sigma must be positive")
    d1 = (log(S / K) + (r - q + 0.5 * sigma * sigma) * T) / (sigma * sqrt(T))
    return float(exp(-q * T) * norm.pdf(d1) / (S * sigma * sqrt(T)))
```

## FAQ

**Why does gamma not depend on whether the option is a call or a put?**

Call minus put is a forward under put-call parity, and a forward's second derivative with respect to spot is zero. Whatever curvature the call has, the put has the same curvature.

**Is a high gamma good?**

It means delta will move quickly if the spot moves, which is a property of that contract in this model. Long gamma and short gamma describe a position. The page does not score either as an advantage.

## Related

- [Delta](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/delta/)
- [Theta](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/theta/)
- [Vega](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vega/)

---

# Vega

> The sensitivity of a European option's Black-Scholes-Merton value to volatility, quoted per volatility point (one percentage point of σ). Call and put vegas of the same contract are equal.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vega/

Category: Options & Derivatives. Term ID: `vega`.

## Definition

Vega is the derivative of the model price with respect to the volatility input. A raw derivative is per 1.00 of σ, that is, per 100 volatility points, which is an awkward unit. Dividing by 100 quotes the change in premium for a one-point move in volatility, the convention used by the Greeks calculator on this site. Because of put-call parity, a European call and put with the same strike and expiry have the same vega: the forward that separates them does not depend on σ.

## Formula

```
ν_raw = S e^{−qT} φ(d1) √T          per 1.00 of volatility
ν     = ν_raw / 100                  per 1 volatility point

d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r − q + σ²/2) T] / (σ √T)
Same value for the European call and the European put.
φ is the standard normal density.
```

## Units

- If the model price rises by 0.375 when volatility goes from 20 percent to 21 percent, vega per point is about 0.375. The raw derivative ∂V/∂σ is about 37.5. This function returns the per-point number.
- The [Greeks calculator](https://quantcore-labs.com/option-greeks-calc/) divides by 100 in the same place. [Implied volatility](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/implied-volatility/) is the σ that the premium implies; vega is how the premium would change if that input changed.
- Call and put share vega for the same reason they share [gamma](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/gamma/): their difference is a forward.

## Pitfalls

- **Volatility point means 0.01 in decimal σ.** Moving σ from 0.20 to 0.21 is one point. Moving it from 0.20 to 1.20 is one hundred points.
- **Sticky strike, sticky delta, and the smile.** The derivative holds every other input fixed, including a single σ. On a smile, a spot move often comes with a different implied volatility. Model vega does not include that.
- **Near expiry, deep in or out of the money, vega is small.** Many vols then fit almost the same premium, which is the same fact as a flat price-versus-σ curve.

## Python reference implementation

Requires scipy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vega/vega.py

```python
from math import exp, log, sqrt
from scipy.stats import norm

def bs_vega(S, K, T, r, sigma, q=0.0) -> float:
    """Black-Scholes-Merton vega per 1 volatility point (dPrice / dσ / 100).

    Same value for a European call and put. S, K, T, sigma must be positive.
    """
    if S <= 0 or K <= 0 or T <= 0 or sigma <= 0:
        raise ValueError("S, K, T and sigma must be positive")
    d1 = (log(S / K) + (r - q + 0.5 * sigma * sigma) * T) / (sigma * sqrt(T))
    return float(S * exp(-q * T) * norm.pdf(d1) * sqrt(T) / 100.0)
```

## FAQ

**Why divide by 100?**

The calculus derivative is the change in price for a change of 1.00 in σ, i.e. from 20 percent to 120 percent. Desks quote the change for one point, from 20 percent to 21 percent, which is that derivative divided by 100. The calculator on this site does the same.

**Do calls and puts have the same vega?**

European calls and puts with the same strike and expiry do, in Black-Scholes-Merton. Put-call parity says their difference does not depend on volatility, so the volatility derivatives match.

## Related

- [Implied Volatility](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/implied-volatility/)
- [Delta](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/delta/)
- [Gamma](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/gamma/)

# Theta

> The sensitivity of a European option's Black-Scholes-Merton value to the passage of calendar time, quoted per day. The annual derivative is divided by 365.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/theta/

Category: Options & Derivatives. Term ID: `theta`.

## Definition

Theta is the derivative of the model value with respect to calendar time, holding spot, volatility, rates and yield fixed. Time to expiry shrinks as calendar time advances, so the formula is minus the derivative with respect to T, then divided by 365 to quote a per-day number. Long options usually have negative theta: the premium decays as expiry approaches, all else equal. That "all else equal" is the catch. Spot and implied volatility do not stay still so that theta can be observed on its own.

## Formula

```
Let φ(d1) be the standard normal density, and
d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r − q + σ²/2) T] / (σ √T),   d2 = d1 − σ √T.

Θ_call = [ −S e^{−qT} φ(d1) σ / (2√T) − r K e^{−rT} N(d2) + q S e^{−qT} N(d1) ] / 365
Θ_put  = [ −S e^{−qT} φ(d1) σ / (2√T) + r K e^{−rT} N(−d2) − q S e^{−qT} N(−d1) ] / 365

Both are per calendar day. A trading-day theta divides the annual derivative by 252 instead;
multiply the value here by 365/252 to convert. q = 0 drops the last term in each bracket.
The Greeks calculator on this site uses these expressions.
```

## What the sign means

- Negative theta means the model value falls as the clock runs, with every other input frozen. That is the usual case for a long option away from unusual rate and dividend combinations.
- The decay term −S e^{−qT} φ(d1) σ / (2√T) is shared. The rate and dividend terms differ for calls and puts, which is why a call theta and a put theta are not equal, unlike [gamma](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/gamma/) and [vega](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vega/).
- See [delta](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/delta/) for the d1 that enters, and the [Greeks calculator](https://quantcore-labs.com/option-greeks-calc/) for the same per-day convention.

## Pitfalls

- **365 versus 252.** This function divides by 365, calendar days, matching the calculator. A desk that marks theta per trading day wants the other divisor. The two numbers differ by 365/252.
- **One day is not infinitesimal.** The derivative times 1/365 approximates the change from losing one calendar day of expiry. Very short-dated options have a theta that changes a lot over that same day, so the approximation is rougher.
- **Frozen volatility.** The derivative does not include a change in implied volatility as expiry approaches. Real premiums move for that reason too.

## Python reference implementation

Requires scipy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/theta/theta.py

```python
from math import exp, log, sqrt
from scipy.stats import norm

def bs_theta(S, K, T, r, sigma, call=True, q=0.0) -> float:
    """Black-Scholes-Merton theta per calendar day (annual derivative / 365).

    call=False returns the put. Multiply by 365/252 for a trading-day theta.
    """
    if S <= 0 or K <= 0 or T <= 0 or sigma <= 0:
        raise ValueError("S, K, T and sigma must be positive")
    sT = sigma * sqrt(T)
    d1 = (log(S / K) + (r - q + 0.5 * sigma * sigma) * T) / sT
    d2 = d1 - sT
    decay = -S * exp(-q * T) * norm.pdf(d1) * sigma / (2.0 * sqrt(T))
    if call:
        annual = decay - r * K * exp(-r * T) * norm.cdf(d2) + q * S * exp(-q * T) * norm.cdf(d1)
    else:
        annual = decay + r * K * exp(-r * T) * norm.cdf(-d2) - q * S * exp(-q * T) * norm.cdf(-d1)
    return float(annual / 365.0)
```

## FAQ

**Why is theta usually negative for a long option?**

With the other inputs held fixed, less time means less chance of a large move and, for a call, less time for the prepaid forward to earn its rates. The model premium of a long option therefore usually falls as expiry gets closer. A short option has the opposite sign. This is a partial derivative, not a prediction of tomorrow's premium.

**Does the function use trading days or calendar days?**

Calendar days. The annual Black-Scholes derivative is divided by 365, which is what the Greeks calculator on this site displays. Multiply by 365/252 if you want a per-trading-day figure.

## Related

- [Delta](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/delta/)
- [Gamma](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/gamma/)
- [Vega](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vega/)

# Rho

> The sensitivity of a European option's Black-Scholes-Merton value to the continuous risk-free rate, quoted per one percentage point of rate.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/rho/

Category: Options & Derivatives. Term ID: `rho`.

## Definition

Rho is the derivative of the model price with respect to the interest rate, holding spot, strike, time, volatility and dividend yield fixed. Dividing by 100 quotes it per one percentage point (from 5 percent to 6 percent, for example), matching the Greeks calculator on this site. A European call's rho is positive: a higher rate lowers the present value of the strike you might pay. A European put's rho is negative. Dividend yield q is a different input and is not what this derivative moves.

## Formula

```
ρ_call = K T e^{−rT} N(d2) / 100
ρ_put  = −K T e^{−rT} N(−d2) / 100

d2 = [ln(S/K) + (r − q − σ²/2) T] / (σ √T)

Per 1 percentage point of r. The raw derivative ∂V/∂r is 100 times larger.
q enters d2. It does not appear as its own discount in the rho formula;
∂V/∂q is a different Greek.
```

## Sign

- Call rho is greater than or equal to zero in this model. Put rho is less than or equal to zero. A book that is long calls and short puts of the same strike picks up both.
- The rate inside Black-Scholes is the continuous risk-free rate used to discount the strike, not a credit spread and not the dividend. Changing q instead is not rho.
- The [Greeks calculator](https://quantcore-labs.com/option-greeks-calc/) reports rho per 1 percent with the formulas above. [Put-call parity](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/put-call-parity/) is where that discount shows up as K e^{−rT}.

## Pitfalls

- **One point of rate, not one point of volatility.** The /100 here is the same kind of unit choice as [vega](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vega/), applied to r rather than to σ.
- **Short-dated options have small rho** because of the factor T. A one-week option barely changes when the rate moves by a point. A five-year option moves much more, in the model.
- **The rate is flat and constant.** A real curve has many rates. One rho cannot describe a shift of a single tenor, a slope change, and a parallel move as three different risks.

## Python reference implementation

Requires scipy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/rho/rho.py

```python
from math import exp, log, sqrt
from scipy.stats import norm

def bs_rho(S, K, T, r, sigma, call=True, q=0.0) -> float:
    """Black-Scholes-Merton rho per 1 percentage point of the risk-free rate.

    call=False returns the put rho, which is negative or zero.
    """
    if S <= 0 or K <= 0 or T <= 0 or sigma <= 0:
        raise ValueError("S, K, T and sigma must be positive")
    d2 = (log(S / K) + (r - q - 0.5 * sigma * sigma) * T) / (sigma * sqrt(T))
    if call:
        return float(K * T * exp(-r * T) * norm.cdf(d2) / 100.0)
    return float(-K * T * exp(-r * T) * norm.cdf(-d2) / 100.0)
```

## FAQ

**Why is put rho negative?**

A higher risk-free rate reduces the present value of the strike the put might receive, and it raises the forward. Both hurt the model value of a European put, so the derivative is negative. A European call is helped by the same two facts.

**Does rho include dividend sensitivity?**

No. q is held fixed. Rho moves only r. The dividend yield changes d2, so a different q produces a different rho, but the derivative itself is with respect to the interest rate.

## Related

- [Delta](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/delta/)
- [Put-Call Parity](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/put-call-parity/)
- [Theta](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/theta/)

# Put-Call Parity

> A model-free relation between European call and put prices that share a strike and an expiry. With a continuous dividend yield, the call minus the put equals the prepaid forward minus the discounted strike.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/put-call-parity/

Category: Options & Derivatives. Term ID: `put-call-parity`.

## Definition

Put-call parity says that a long European call and a short European put, same strike and expiry, replicate a long forward position struck at K. Rearranged, the call premium minus the put premium equals the spot discounted by the dividend yield, minus the strike discounted by the interest rate. No volatility, no distribution of returns and no pricing model enters. If the two premiums violate the equation by more than transaction costs, the packages are different prices for the same payoff. The function returns the gap, which is zero when parity holds.

## Formula

```
C − P = S e^{−qT} − K e^{−rT}

q = 0 (no dividends):   C − P = S − K e^{−rT}
gap = (C − P) − (S e^{−qT} − K e^{−rT})

gap = 0  → parity holds at these inputs
gap > 0  → the call is rich to the put, or the forward is cheap, relative to this identity
The identity is for European options. American options do not obey it as an equality.
```

## What it constrains

- You can back a forward out of the two premiums, which is what the [smile tool](https://quantcore-labs.com/tools/iv-smile/) does before it reads a smile off strikes. A bad forward makes every implied volatility look skewed.
- It forces several Greeks into pairs. Differentiating in S gives Δ_call − Δ_put = e^{−qT} ([delta](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/delta/)). Differentiating in σ gives equal [vegas](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vega/). Differentiating twice in S gives equal [gammas](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/gamma/).
- [Rho](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/rho/) is the sensitivity to the r that discounts K in this identity.

## Pitfalls

- **European, same strike, same expiry, same underlying.** An American put can be worth more than parity allows, because early exercise has value. A gap on American prices is not automatically an arbitrage.
- **Dividends have to be in q, or the identity is the wrong one.** A discrete cash dividend is not a continuous yield. Using q = 0 on a stock that pays a dividend shows a gap that is just the dividend.
- **Costs.** A gap smaller than the round-trip spread, fees and borrow is not a trade. The function returns a price difference, not an executable profit.

## Python reference implementation

Requires standard library. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/put-call-parity/put-call-parity.py

```python
from math import exp

def parity_gap(call, put, S, K, T, r, q=0.0) -> float:
    """Call minus put, minus the European forward value S*exp(-qT) - K*exp(-rT).

    Zero when put-call parity holds. Not defined as an equality for American options.
    """
    if S <= 0 or K <= 0 or T < 0:
        raise ValueError("S and K must be positive and T non-negative")
    return float((call - put) - (S * exp(-q * T) - K * exp(-r * T)))
```

## FAQ

**Why does parity not mention volatility?**

The call-minus-put package pays S_T − K at expiry no matter what path volatility takes. Its present value is the prepaid forward minus the discounted strike. Volatility changes the call and the put by the same amount, so it drops out of the difference.

**What does a non-zero gap mean?**

At these inputs the two premiums are not consistent with one forward. Causes include a dividend yield you left at zero, American early exercise, stale quotes, or a genuine dislocation larger than the cost of putting the package on. The sign says which side is rich relative to the identity. It does not by itself say there is a trade.

## Related

- [Implied Volatility](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/implied-volatility/)
- [Delta](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/delta/)
- [Rho](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/rho/)
