# Half-Life of Mean Reversion

> How many periods an AR(1) deviation takes to decay halfway, read off the slope of a regression of changes on lagged levels. The same discrete definition as the half-life on the ADF page.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/half-life-mean-reversion/

Category: Time Series & Stat-Arb. Term ID: `half-life-mean-reversion`.

## Definition

Fit the regression Δy_t = a + g y_{t−1} + ε_t. The autoregressive level coefficient is φ = 1 + g. When g is between −1 and 0, the series pulls back toward its mean, and the number of periods required for a deviation to fall by half is ln 2 / −ln(1 + g). That is the discrete half-life. The continuous approximation −ln 2 / g is close only when g is near zero; at φ = 0.9 it is already about 5 percent longer than the discrete number. If g is not negative, the series is not mean-reverting on this regression and the half-life is infinite.

## Formula

```
Δy_t = a + g · y_{t−1} + ε_t
φ = 1 + g

half-life = ln(2) / −ln(1 + g)     if −1 < g < 0
          = ∞                       if g ≥ 0
          undefined (NaN)           if g ≤ −1  (oscillatory or explosive)

Continuous approximation, small g:  ln(2) / −g
Example: φ = 0.9 → g = −0.1 → half-life = ln(2) / −ln(0.9) ≈ 6.58 periods.
The ADF page uses this discrete definition, not ln(2) / −g.
```

## Where the number is used

- As a holding-period scale for a spread that has already passed a stationarity check. See [ADF](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/adf-test/) and [cointegration](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/cointegration/). A half-life of six days and a half-life of six months are different research problems.
- As a way to set the window on a [rolling z-score](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/pairs-zscore-signal/). A window much shorter than the half-life mostly fits noise; a window of many half-lives averages different regimes.
- [Hurst](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/hurst-exponent/) is a related but different summary of the same wish: H below one half suggests anti-persistence. It is not a half-life.

## Pitfalls

- **Use the discrete form.** Dividing ln 2 by −g treats g as a continuous-time speed. The regression you just ran is discrete. This function matches the half-life already published on the ADF page, ln 2 / −ln(1+g).
- **The regression is not a proof of mean reversion.** A short sample of a random walk often produces a slightly negative g. Pair the half-life with an ADF or cointegration test, and expect the estimate to move when you add data.
- **An intercept is included.** The mean that the series reverts to is −a/g, not necessarily zero. Forcing the regression through the origin changes g.
- **Not a trading rule.** A finite half-life is a sample statistic. It does not say the spread will keep reverting, or that a position sized to it is desirable.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/half-life-mean-reversion/half-life-mean-reversion.py

```python
import numpy as np

def half_life(spread) -> float:
    """Discrete mean-reversion half-life, ln(2) / -ln(1+g), from Δy = a + g y_lag.

    Infinite when g >= 0 (no mean reversion). NaN when g <= -1.
    Same definition as half_life on the ADF page.
    """
    y = np.asarray(spread, dtype=float)
    if y.ndim != 1 or y.size < 3 or not np.all(np.isfinite(y)):
        raise ValueError("need at least three finite observations")
    lag = y[:-1]
    if float(np.var(lag)) == 0.0:
        return float("inf")
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(lag.size), lag])
    g = float(np.linalg.lstsq(X, np.diff(y), rcond=None)[0][1])
    if g >= -1e-12:
        return float("inf")
    if g <= -1.0:
        return float("nan")
    return float(np.log(2.0) / -np.log1p(g))
```

## FAQ

**Why not use −ln(2) / g, which is the formula many notes quote?**

That is the continuous-time limit. The regression Δy_t = a + g y_{t−1} implies a discrete autoregressive coefficient φ = 1 + g, and a deviation multiplies by φ each period. Halving means φ^h = 1/2, so h = ln(2) / −ln(φ). At φ = 0.9 the continuous shortcut is about 6.93 periods and the discrete half-life is about 6.58.

**What half-life should a pairs trade use?**

This page does not pick one. It estimates a half-life from the series you pass. Whether the residual is stationary, whether both legs can be traded, and what it costs are separate questions; a finite estimate is not a signal to trade the spread.

## Related

- [Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) Test](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/adf-test/)
- [Cointegration (Engle-Granger & Johansen)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/cointegration/)
- [Hurst Exponent (H)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/hurst-exponent/)
- [Rolling Hedge Ratio and Spread Z-Score](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/pairs-zscore-signal/)

# Fast Rolling Mean, Std, Beta and Z-score with Numba

> O(n) rolling mean, standard deviation, OLS beta and 2-D z-score compiled with Numba. In tests here they run 4 to 7 times faster than pandas and are more accurate on large-valued series.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/rolling-window-numba/

Category: High-Performance Python. Snippet ID: `rolling-window-numba`.

## What it does

These functions compute rolling statistics with running sums in a single compiled pass, instead of recomputing each window. Values are re-centred on the first window's mean, which avoids the catastrophic cancellation that running sums suffer on series with large levels, such as prices or index points. Numba compiles plain Python loops to machine code, so there is no build step: install with pip and call the functions on NumPy arrays.

## Approach

```
Running sums over the window, after centring v = x − c:
  S₁ += v_new − v_old       S₂ += v_new² − v_old²
  mean = S₁/w + c            var = (S₂ − w·(S₁/w)²) / (w − 1)
  beta = (S_xy − S_x·S_y/w) / (S_xx − S_x²/w)

Measured here, 1,000,000 points, window 250 (mean + std + beta):  Numba ≈ 20 ms, pandas ≈ 135 ms
2,000 × 500 matrix, rolling z-score, window 60:                   Numba ≈ 11 ms, pandas ≈ 52 ms
Max relative std error vs exact two-pass:                         Numba 1.6e−9, pandas 2.2e−8
```

## When to use it

- Long minute-bar or tick series where pandas rolling is the bottleneck.
- Rolling hedge ratios for [pairs](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/cointegration/), and rolling z-scores across a whole stock universe in one call.
- Inside larger Numba-compiled backtest loops, since these functions can be called from other `@njit` code.

## Pitfalls

- **NaN handling.** The inputs must be NaN-free. Running sums propagate a NaN forever. Fill, drop or split around gaps first.
- **Compile time.** The first call compiles, which takes about a second. `cache=True` stores the compiled code next to the file so later runs start instantly.
- **Numerical drift.** Without centring, the variance of a series around 10,000 loses most of its significant digits. If the level changes enormously over the sample, re-centre periodically.
- **Parallelism.** For very wide matrices, switch the column loop in `rolling_zscore_2d` to `numba.prange` with `parallel=True`.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy, numba. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/rolling-window-numba/rolling-window-numba.py

```python
import numpy as np
from numba import njit

@njit(cache=True)
def rolling_mean_std(x, window):
    """O(n) rolling mean and sample std (ddof=1) with running sums.
    Values are re-centred on the first window's mean to limit cancellation error.
    NaN where fewer than `window` observations; input must contain no NaN."""
    n = x.shape[0]
    mean = np.full(n, np.nan)
    std = np.full(n, np.nan)
    if n < window:
        return mean, std
    shift = x[:window].mean()
    s = 0.0
    s2 = 0.0
    for i in range(n):
        v = x[i] - shift
        s += v
        s2 += v * v
        if i >= window:
            o = x[i - window] - shift
            s -= o
            s2 -= o * o
        if i >= window - 1:
            m = s / window
            mean[i] = m + shift
            var = (s2 - window * m * m) / (window - 1)
            std[i] = np.sqrt(var) if var > 0 else 0.0
    return mean, std

@njit(cache=True)
def rolling_beta(y, x, window):
    """Rolling OLS slope cov(y, x) / var(x), O(n). Use for hedge ratios or market beta.
    Inputs are re-centred on their first-window means to limit cancellation error."""
    n = y.shape[0]
    out = np.full(n, np.nan)
    if n < window:
        return out
    cx = x[:window].mean()
    cy = y[:window].mean()
    sx = sy = sxx = sxy = 0.0
    for i in range(n):
        a = x[i] - cx
        b = y[i] - cy
        sx += a; sy += b; sxx += a * a; sxy += a * b
        if i >= window:
            a = x[i - window] - cx
            b = y[i - window] - cy
            sx -= a; sy -= b; sxx -= a * a; sxy -= a * b
        if i >= window - 1:
            cov = sxy - sx * sy / window
            var = sxx - sx * sx / window
            if var > 0:
                out[i] = cov / var
    return out

@njit(cache=True)
def rolling_zscore_2d(X, window):
    """Rolling z-score for every column of a (T x N) float matrix, in one compiled pass."""
    T, N = X.shape
    Z = np.full((T, N), np.nan)
    for j in range(N):
        m, s = rolling_mean_std(X[:, j].copy(), window)
        for i in range(T):
            if s[i] > 0:
                Z[i, j] = (X[i, j] - m[i]) / s[i]
    return Z
```

## FAQ

**Why Numba instead of Cython?**

Numba needs no compiler toolchain or build step: decorate a function and it is compiled on first call. Performance for simple numeric loops is comparable to Cython, and the code stays plain Python that can be copied and run directly.

**Is pandas rolling not already fast?**

pandas rolling is implemented in Cython and is fine for most work, but each statistic is a separate pass with object overhead, and combinations such as rolling beta need several calls. A single fused Numba pass was 4–7× faster in the benchmarks above.

- [Cointegration (Engle-Granger & Johansen)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/cointegration/)
- [Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) Test](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/adf-test/)

# Query Tick Data in Parquet with DuckDB

> Build 1-minute OHLCV and VWAP bars, and daily turnover, straight from Hive-partitioned tick Parquet files with DuckDB. There is no database server and no loading step, and filters skip unneeded files and row groups.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/duckdb-parquet-ticks/

Category: Data Engineering for Quants. Snippet ID: `duckdb-parquet-ticks`.

## What it does

DuckDB is an in-process analytical database that queries Parquet files in place. With one folder per trading day (Hive partitioning), a date filter skips whole folders. Sorting rows by stock code inside each file lets Parquet's row-group min/max statistics skip most of the data for a code filter. The snippet shows the storage layout, a writer that produces it, and queries for minute bars and daily turnover.

## Approach

```
Layout:  ticks/date=YYYY-MM-DD/part-0.parquet   (ts, seq, code, price, volume)

read_parquet('ticks/*/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = true)
  WHERE date BETWEEN ? AND ?      → partition pruning (folders never opened)
    AND code IN (...)             → row-group pruning via min/max statistics

open  = arg_min(price, (ts, seq))      close = arg_max(price, (ts, seq))
vwap  = Σ price·volume / Σ volume       bucket = time_bucket(INTERVAL 1 MINUTE, ts)
```

## Why this layout

- **One partition per day** matches how tick data arrives and how research queries are scoped. Adding a day means writing one new folder.
- **Sorted by code, zstd-compressed.** This gives small files and effective code filters. Avoid thousands of tiny files: aim for one to a few files per day.
- The same files are readable by pandas, Polars and Spark, so there is no lock-in.

## Pitfalls

- **Timestamp ties.** Several ticks often share one timestamp. Ordering by `ts` alone picked the wrong open or close in 27–30% of minutes in the test for this page. Always carry the exchange sequence number and order by `(ts, seq)`.
- **Auction ticks.** A-share opening (09:15–09:25) and closing (14:57–15:00) call-auction prints are single-price matches. Decide whether bars include them, and filter by time if not.
- **Time zones.** Store exchange-local timestamps consistently, either naive local time or TIMESTAMPTZ, but never mixed.
- **Partition column type.** Hive values are parsed from folder names. Compare against values of the same type, and check with `DESCRIBE`.

## Python reference implementation

Requires duckdb. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/duckdb-parquet-ticks/duckdb-parquet-ticks.py

```python
import duckdb

# Layout this snippet assumes (Hive partitioning, one folder per trading day):
#   ticks/date=2024-03-01/part-0.parquet    columns: ts TIMESTAMP, seq BIGINT, code VARCHAR, price DOUBLE, volume BIGINT
# seq = exchange sequence number. Several ticks often share one timestamp, so open/close
# must be ordered by (ts, seq); ordering by ts alone picks an arbitrary tick on ties.
#   ticks/date=2024-03-04/part-0.parquet    ...

def connect(threads: int = 0) -> duckdb.DuckDBPyConnection:
    con = duckdb.connect()                      # in-memory; Parquet stays on disk
    if threads:
        con.execute(f"SET threads = {threads}")
    return con

def minute_bars(con, root: str, codes: list, start: str, end: str):
    """1-minute OHLCV + VWAP straight from tick Parquet.
    The date filter prunes whole partition folders and the code filter is pushed down
    to Parquet row-group statistics, so only the needed bytes are read."""
    return con.execute(f"""
        SELECT code,
               time_bucket(INTERVAL 1 MINUTE, ts)   AS minute,
               arg_min(price, (ts, seq))             AS open,
               max(price)                            AS high,
               min(price)                            AS low,
               arg_max(price, (ts, seq))             AS close,
               sum(volume)                           AS volume,
               sum(price * volume) / sum(volume)     AS vwap
        FROM read_parquet('{root}/*/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = true)
        WHERE date BETWEEN ? AND ? AND code IN (SELECT unnest(?))
        GROUP BY ALL
        ORDER BY code, minute
    """, [start, end, codes]).df()

def daily_turnover(con, root: str, start: str, end: str):
    """Per-stock daily traded value, e.g. the 'amount' input for the Amihud measure."""
    return con.execute(f"""
        SELECT date, code, sum(price * volume) AS amount
        FROM read_parquet('{root}/*/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = true)
        WHERE date BETWEEN ? AND ?
        GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY date, code
    """, [start, end]).df()

def write_partitioned(con, df, root: str):
    """Write a pandas DataFrame with a 'date' column as Hive-partitioned, zstd Parquet,
    sorted by code so row-group min/max statistics make code filters effective."""
    con.register("src", df)
    con.execute(f"""COPY (SELECT * FROM src ORDER BY date, code, ts, seq)
                    TO '{root}' (FORMAT parquet, PARTITION_BY (date), COMPRESSION zstd, OVERWRITE_OR_IGNORE)""")
    con.unregister("src")
```

## FAQ

**Why DuckDB instead of loading everything into pandas?**

DuckDB reads only the partitions, columns and row groups a query needs, runs multi-threaded, and spills to disk when data exceeds memory. Tens of millions of ticks that would not fit comfortably in a pandas DataFrame can be aggregated directly from Parquet.

**Should I store ticks in a .duckdb file or in Parquet?**

Both work. Parquet is open, portable across pandas/Polars/Spark and easy to append by day; a .duckdb database file is convenient for derived tables and indexes. A common pattern is raw ticks in partitioned Parquet and derived bars or factors in a DuckDB file.

## Related

- [Amihud Illiquidity Measure (ILLIQ)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/amihud-illiquidity/)
- [Volume-Weighted Average Price (VWAP)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vwap/)

# Vectorised Daily Backtest with A-share Trading Constraints

> A daily long-only backtest core that vectorises over the whole stock universe. It blocks look-ahead by construction and handles suspensions, limit-up and limit-down untradability and turnover costs. A Polars version is included for the unconstrained case.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/vectorized-backtest/

Category: Backtesting. Snippet ID: `vectorized-backtest`.

## What it does

The backtest turns a dates × stocks boolean signal into equal-weight holdings and daily net returns. Every operation is vectorised across stocks. Only the loop over dates remains, because whether a stock can be bought or sold today depends on what is already held: a stock stuck at limit-down cannot be sold and stays in the book. Orders decided at the close of day t execute at the close of t+1, so a signal can never use the return it trades on.

## Approach

```
Timing:   signal[t] (data ≤ close t) → order at close t+1 → earns close(t+1) → close(t+2)

want_t    = signal_{t−1}
held_t    = enter if want ∧ ¬held ∧ buyable_t ;  exit if ¬want ∧ held ∧ sellable_t
weight_t  = held_t / Σ held_t
gross_t   = Σ_i weight_{t−1,i} · r_{t,i}
turnover_t= Σ_i |weight_{t,i} − weight_{t−1,i}|
net_t     = gross_t − turnover_t · cost_bps / 10⁴
```

## What the tests check

- Net returns match a naive per-stock, per-day loop to within 1e−17.
- The Polars version matches the pandas version when every stock is tradable.
- **Look-ahead probe.** Two hypothetical signals were run. One uses only the next day's return, which this timing can never capture; it earns about zero (0.03% per day, which is noise). The other uses the return two days ahead, which this timing does capture; it earns 1.6% per day, the size of gain that look-ahead leaks would produce.

## Pitfalls

- **Costs.** A-share stamp duty is charged on sells only (0.05% since 28 August 2023), plus commission and slippage. A single symmetric `cost_bps` is an approximation; use separate buy and sell rates for precision.
- **Prices.** Use dividend- and split-adjusted closes, such as back-adjusted 后复权 prices, or returns will show false jumps.
- **Survivorship.** Include delisted stocks and the universe as it was on each date, not today's constituents.
- **Close execution is optimistic.** Trading exactly at the close ignores closing-auction impact. Stress-test with next-day VWAP or open execution.
- **Tradability flags.** Derive limit-up and limit-down from the previous close and the board's limit (±10% main board, ±20% ChiNext/STAR, ±5% ST). A close at the limit price is the usual proxy for "could not trade in that direction".

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy, pandas, polars. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/vectorized-backtest/vectorized-backtest.py

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def backtest(signal: pd.DataFrame, close: pd.DataFrame, tradable_buy: pd.DataFrame,
             tradable_sell: pd.DataFrame, cost_bps: float = 15.0) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Daily long-only, equal-weight backtest, dates x stocks, no Python loop over assets.

    signal[t]        : True = want to hold, decided with data up to the close of t
    tradable_buy[t]  : can buy at the close of t   (A-shares: not suspended, not at limit-up)
    tradable_sell[t] : can sell at the close of t  (not suspended, not at limit-down)
    Orders for signal[t] execute at the close of t+1; returns are close-to-close.
    cost_bps is charged on one-way turnover (commission + stamp duty + slippage)."""
    want = signal.shift(1).fillna(False).astype(bool)          # no look-ahead
    held = np.zeros(signal.shape[1], dtype=bool)
    hold = np.zeros(signal.shape, dtype=bool)
    tb, ts, w = tradable_buy.to_numpy(bool), tradable_sell.to_numpy(bool), want.to_numpy(bool)
    for t in range(len(signal)):                                # loop over dates only
        held = np.where(w[t] & ~held & tb[t], True, held)       # enter if allowed
        held = np.where(~w[t] & held & ts[t], False, held)      # exit if allowed (else stuck)
        hold[t] = held
    n = hold.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    weight = pd.DataFrame(np.divide(hold, n, out=np.zeros(hold.shape), where=n > 0),
                          index=signal.index, columns=signal.columns)
    ret = close.pct_change(fill_method=None).fillna(0.0)
    gross = (weight.shift(1).fillna(0.0) * ret).sum(axis=1)      # weight set at close t earns t+1
    turnover = weight.diff().abs().sum(axis=1).fillna(weight.abs().sum(axis=1))
    net = gross - turnover * cost_bps / 1e4
    return pd.DataFrame({"gross": gross, "turnover": turnover, "net": net,
                         "equity": (1 + net).cumprod(), "n_held": n.ravel()})

def backtest_polars(signal_long, cost_bps: float = 15.0):
    """Polars version for the simple case (always tradable) on long data with columns
    date, code, close, signal. Same timing convention as backtest()."""
    import polars as pl
    df = (signal_long.sort("code", "date")
          .with_columns(want=pl.col("signal").shift(1).over("code").fill_null(False),
                        ret=(pl.col("close") / pl.col("close").shift(1) - 1).over("code").fill_null(0.0))
          .with_columns(n=pl.col("want").sum().over("date"))
          .with_columns(weight=pl.when(pl.col("n") > 0).then(pl.col("want").cast(pl.Float64) / pl.col("n")).otherwise(0.0))
          .with_columns(w_prev=pl.col("weight").shift(1).over("code").fill_null(0.0)))
    daily = (df.group_by("date").agg(gross=(pl.col("w_prev") * pl.col("ret")).sum(),
                                     turnover=(pl.col("weight") - pl.col("w_prev")).abs().sum())
             .sort("date")
             .with_columns(net=pl.col("gross") - pl.col("turnover") * cost_bps / 1e4))
    return daily.with_columns(equity=(1 + pl.col("net")).cum_prod())
```

## FAQ

**Why is there still a loop over dates?**

Holdings are path-dependent once trading constraints exist: a stock at limit-down cannot be sold, so whether it is held today depends on yesterday's holdings. The loop runs over dates only, with every operation inside vectorised across the whole universe, so a 20-year daily backtest on 5,000 stocks is about 5,000 vectorised steps.

**How do I avoid look-ahead bias?**

Shift every signal by at least one period before it can affect positions, and decide the execution price in advance. In this code a signal formed at the close of t trades at the close of t+1 and first earns the t+1 to t+2 return; the test suite checks that a signal built from the t to t+1 return earns nothing.

## Related

- [Information Coefficient (IC)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/information-coefficient/)
- [Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/var-expected-shortfall/)
- [Amihud Illiquidity Measure (ILLIQ)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/amihud-illiquidity/)

# O(n) Rolling Mean (Cython Memoryview Recurrence)

> The expanding-then-fixed rolling mean from a boundscheck-free Cython memoryview loop, implemented here with a NumPy prefix sum so the generator can re-execute it. The Cython source is included for compilation on a machine with a C toolchain.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/cython-rolling-mean/

Category: High-Performance Python. Snippet ID: `cython-rolling-mean`.

## What it does

A rolling mean can be updated by adding the new observation and subtracting the one that left the window, which is a single pass. Before the window is full the same sum is divided by the number of observations seen so far. The Cython form types the buffer as a double memoryview and turns bounds checks off. This page publishes that recurrence as a tested NumPy function, plus the Cython source as a string, because this site's generator executes every snippet with CPython and cannot compile cimport.

## Approach

```
Let s_−1 = 0. For i = 0..n−1:
  s_i = s_{i−1} + x_i − x_{i−w} · 1{i ≥ w}
  m_i = s_i / w            if i ≥ w
      = s_i / (i+1)        if i < w

Prefix-sum form (same values):
  m_i = (c_i − c_{i−w}) / w    for i ≥ w,   c_i = Σ_{k=0..i} x_k,  c_{<0} = 0
  m_i = c_i / (i+1)            for i < w

Cython sketch (compile with cythonize; not executed by the generator):
  @cython.boundscheck(False)
  @cython.wraparound(False)
  def fast_rolling_mean(double[:] arr, int window): ...
```

## When to use it

- One rolling mean over a long tick or bar array, where a Python per-window loop is the cost and a C compiler is available for the memoryview version.
- As a readable specification of the partial-window convention (divide by `i+1` until the window is full, then by `w`). The NumPy function is what the tests lock in.
- For several rolling statistics at once, or for prices with a large level, the centred running sums in [rolling-window-numba](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/rolling-window-numba/) are a better fit. They need no compiler and lose less precision.

## Pitfalls

- **This page does not compile Cython.** `cimport` is not valid Python, so shipping only the memoryview function would fail the rebuild test. `CYTHON_SOURCE` is the compiled form; `fast_rolling_mean` is the reference.
- **Cancellation.** A raw running sum of prices near 10,000 loses digits in the variance, and even the mean drifts once the sum is huge. Re-centre, or use the Numba operators, if the level is large relative to the variation inside the window.
- **NaNs.** One NaN stays inside the prefix sum from that index onward. Drop or fill gaps first.
- **Window edges.** Index `i = w−1` is still the mean of the first `w` points. Index `i = w` drops `x_0`. Callers who want NaN during the warm-up should mask `i < w−1` themselves.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/cython-rolling-mean/cython-rolling-mean.py

```python
import numpy as np

# Same recurrence as a Cython loop over a double memoryview. Compile CYTHON_SOURCE
# with Cython (boundscheck and wraparound off) when a C compiler is available.
# The function below is the tested reference: CPython cannot execute cimport.
CYTHON_SOURCE = """
cimport cython
import numpy as np

@cython.boundscheck(False)
@cython.wraparound(False)
def fast_rolling_mean(double[:] arr, int window):
    cdef int n = arr.shape[0]
    cdef double[:] res = np.empty(n)
    cdef double s = 0.0
    cdef int i
    for i in range(n):
        s += arr[i]
        if i >= window:
            s -= arr[i - window]
            res[i] = s / window
        else:
            res[i] = s / (i + 1)
    return np.asarray(res)
"""

def fast_rolling_mean(arr, window: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """Rolling mean. Partial windows divide by the number of points seen so far.

    For i >= window the result is the mean of x[i-window+1 : i+1].
    Equivalent to the memoryview loop in CYTHON_SOURCE.
    """
    x = np.ascontiguousarray(arr, dtype=np.float64).reshape(-1)
    window = int(window)
    if window < 1:
        raise ValueError("window must be a positive integer")
    n = x.size
    out = np.empty(n, dtype=np.float64)
    if n == 0:
        return out
    csum = np.cumsum(x)
    np.divide(csum, np.arange(1, n + 1, dtype=np.float64), out=out)
    if n > window:
        out[window:] = (csum[window:] - csum[:-window]) / window
    return out
```

## FAQ

**Why is the published function NumPy rather than Cython?**

The site rebuilds by executing every snippet with Python. Cython syntax such as cimport and cdef does not run there, and a C compiler is not part of the rebuild. The NumPy prefix sum matches the memoryview loop value for value; the Cython source is in the same file for when you compile it locally.

**How is this different from the Numba rolling operators?**

This recurrence is a single mean, including a defined value on the warm-up samples. The Numba snippet computes mean, sample standard deviation, rolling beta and a 2-D z-score, re-centres to protect precision, and leaves the warm-up as NaN.

- [Rolling Z-Score from a Zero-Copy Sliding Window](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/numpy-strided-rolling/)

# Load Hive-Partitioned Parquet Ticks with Bound Parameters

> Read a date slice of tick Parquet through DuckDB. The file glob and the date are bound parameters, so a path or a date string cannot change the SQL.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/duckdb-parquet-loader/

Category: Data Engineering for Quants. Snippet ID: `duckdb-parquet-loader`.

## What it does

DuckDB queries Parquet in place. With Hive layout (one folder per day), a predicate on the partition column skips other days. The glob passed to read_parquet and the date in the WHERE clause are both placeholders. Building either value into the SQL text with an f-string would let a quote in a path, or a crafted date, close the string and append another statement. Binding them does not.

## Approach

```
Layout:  ticks/date=YYYY-MM-DD/part-*.parquet
Columns: timestamp, symbol, price, volume

SELECT symbol, timestamp, price, volume
FROM read_parquet(?, hive_partitioning = true)   -- ? = glob, not an interpolated path
WHERE date = ?                                   -- ? = the date
  AND volume > 0
ORDER BY timestamp
```

## Why bind every value

- The date filter is what makes a Hive layout useful: folders outside the day are not opened. It only stays a filter if it is a value, not a piece of SQL text.
- Paths from a config file, a request, or a folder name with a quote are data. `read_parquet(?)` passes them through DuckDB's parameter API.
- For minute bars, VWAP and code filters on the same layout, see [duckdb-parquet-ticks](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/duckdb-parquet-ticks/).

## Pitfalls

- **Partition type.** Hive values are parsed from folder names. `date=2024-03-01` usually arrives as a date. Compare it to a date or an ISO date string, and check with `DESCRIBE` if a filter suddenly matches nothing.
- **Zero-size prints.** The query drops `volume <= 0`. Those rows are not trades. Decide separately whether auction prints belong in the extract.
- **Glob, not a Python path join inside SQL.** Pass the glob from Python (`dir/**/*.parquet`). Do not concatenate it into the query string.

## Python reference implementation

Requires duckdb. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/duckdb-parquet-loader/duckdb-parquet-loader.py

```python
import duckdb

def query_ticks_by_date(parquet_glob: str, target_date: str):
    """Ticks for one Hive date partition.

    parquet_glob and target_date are bound parameters. They are never
    interpolated into the SQL text.
    """
    if not isinstance(parquet_glob, str) or not isinstance(target_date, str):
        raise TypeError("parquet_glob and target_date must be strings")
    if parquet_glob == "" or target_date == "":
        raise ValueError("parquet_glob and target_date must be non-empty")
    con = duckdb.connect()
    return con.execute(
        """
        SELECT symbol, timestamp, price, volume
        FROM read_parquet(?, hive_partitioning = true)
        WHERE date = ?
          AND volume > 0
        ORDER BY timestamp
        """,
        [parquet_glob, target_date],
    ).df()
```

## FAQ

**Why not use an f-string for the path?**

read_parquet needs a path, and an f-string is the obvious way to supply it, but the path then becomes SQL syntax. A directory name containing a quote breaks the query or changes it. A bound parameter keeps the path as a value. The same applies to the date.

**Does this load the whole dataset into memory?**

DuckDB reads the Parquet row groups required by the query. A selective date predicate on a Hive partition avoids opening other days. The result of this particular query is still a pandas DataFrame of every matching tick, so aggregate in SQL when the day is large. See the minute-bar query on the DuckDB ticks page.

## Related

- [Query Tick Data in Parquet with DuckDB](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/duckdb-parquet-ticks/)
- [Per-Symbol Minute VWAP in DuckDB](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/duckdb-asof-vwap/)
- [Resample Trade Ticks to OHLCV and VWAP Bars](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/pandas-tick-to-ohlcv/)

# Polars Moving-Average Crossover, Lagged One Bar

> A moving-average crossover in Polars lazy expressions. The position is shifted one bar so it cannot earn the return that formed the signal, and a cost is charged when the position changes. Educational example only.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/polars-vectorized-backtest/

Category: Backtesting. Snippet ID: `polars-vectorized-backtest`.

## What it does

The signal is long when the fast mean of close is above the slow mean, and flat otherwise. That decision is delayed by one bar before it multiplies returns, which is the minimum delay that removes same-bar look-ahead on a close-to-close return. Turnover is the absolute change in position. Cost is turnover times a constant in basis points. This is a single-series illustration, not a portfolio backtest and not a trading recommendation.

## Approach

```
ret_t     = C_t / C_{t−1} − 1
signal_t  = 1{ MA_fast(C)_t > MA_slow(C)_t }     (0 while either mean is null)
pos_t     = signal_{t−1}                         (0 at t = 0)
cost_t    = |pos_t − pos_{t−1}| · cost_bps / 10^4
strat_t   = pos_t · ret_t − cost_t
equity_t  = Π_{s≤t} (1 + strat_s)

Warm-up bars, where a mean is missing, contribute signal 0.
```

## What the lag does

- The means at bar t use the close of bar t. The return of bar t is the move from t−1 to t, which is already in that close. Multiplying them on the same row would book a fill at a price the signal has already used.
- `shift(1)` applies the decision from bar t to the return of bar t+1: the earliest close-to-close return that starts after the signal.
- For a dates × stocks book with suspensions and limit-up or limit-down flags, use [vectorized-backtest](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/vectorized-backtest/). This page is one series and no trading constraints.

## Pitfalls

- **Costs are a flat bps charge.** There is no spread, no impact and no borrow. A crossover that looks fine here can be negative once those are added.
- **One position, all or nothing.** The position is 0 or 1. It does not size by volatility or cap turnover.
- **Adjusted prices.** Splits and dividends have to be in the close series already. A raw close series invents returns on corporate actions.
- **This is not a forecast.** A historical equity curve of a moving-average rule is a description of that sample. It is not evidence that the rule will make money on the next sample.

## Python reference implementation

Requires polars. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/polars-vectorized-backtest/polars-vectorized-backtest.py

```python
import polars as pl

def ma_crossover_backtest(df: pl.DataFrame, fast: int = 20, slow: int = 100, cost_bps: float = 1.0) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Moving-average crossover on columns timestamp, close.

    The position implied by bar t is applied to the return of bar t+1.
    cost_bps is charged on the absolute change in position.
    Educational example only; not a trading strategy.
    """
    if fast < 1 or slow < 1:
        raise ValueError("fast and slow windows must be positive")
    if cost_bps < 0:
        raise ValueError("cost_bps must be non-negative")
    ready = pl.col("fast_ma").is_not_null() & pl.col("slow_ma").is_not_null()
    signal = pl.when(ready & (pl.col("fast_ma") > pl.col("slow_ma"))).then(1.0).otherwise(0.0)
    return (
        df.lazy()
        .sort("timestamp")
        .with_columns(
            ret=pl.col("close").pct_change(),
            fast_ma=pl.col("close").rolling_mean(fast),
            slow_ma=pl.col("close").rolling_mean(slow),
        )
        .with_columns(pos=signal.shift(1).fill_null(0.0))
        .with_columns(cost=pl.col("pos").diff().abs().fill_null(0.0) * cost_bps / 1e4)
        .with_columns(strat_ret=pl.col("pos") * pl.col("ret").fill_null(0.0) - pl.col("cost"))
        .with_columns(equity=(1 + pl.col("strat_ret")).cum_prod())
        .collect()
    )
```

## FAQ

**Why is the position shifted by one bar?**

The close that updates the moving averages is the same close that ends the bar's return. Using the signal on that same return treats the bar as both the information and the fill. The shift makes the signal wait for the next return.

**Does a higher equity curve mean the rule works?**

No. The curve is the result of this rule, this cost and this sample, with no market impact. Use it to check the code. Judging whether a rule is worth trading needs a later sample, realistic costs and a risk report.

## Related

- [Vectorised Daily Backtest with A-share Trading Constraints](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/vectorized-backtest/)
- [Sharpe Ratio](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/sharpe-ratio/)
- [Maximum Drawdown](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/max-drawdown/)

# RiskMetrics EWMA Volatility in Numba

> Exponentially weighted variance compiled with Numba. The variance at t uses returns only through t−1, so the latest shock is not included in the volatility assigned to that same index.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/numba-ewma-volatility/

Category: High-Performance Python. Snippet ID: `numba-ewma-volatility`.

## What it does

RiskMetrics writes today's variance as a blend of yesterday's variance and yesterday's squared return. The weight on the previous variance is λ, often 0.94 for daily data. The square root of that variance is the EWMA volatility. The loop is a prefix recursion, which Numba compiles to a tight machine-code pass. It is a smoother with a fixed λ, not a fitted GARCH model.

## Approach

```
σ²_0 = r_0²
σ²_t = λ σ²_{t−1} + (1 − λ) r_{t−1}²     t = 1..n−1
σ_t  = sqrt(σ²_t)

σ_t depends on r_0 .. r_{t−1} only.
0 ≤ λ ≤ 1.  λ = 1 repeats σ²_0.  λ = 0 gives σ²_t = r_{t−1}².
```

## When to use it

- A causal volatility estimate on a long return series, for scaling positions or for comparing with [realized volatility](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/realized-volatility/).
- Inside another `@njit` loop. A Python EWMA over millions of bars spends its time in the interpreter; this one does not, after the first compile.
- For a variance that also reacts to a long-run level and is estimated rather than set, see [GARCH(1,1)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/garch/).

## Pitfalls

- **Initial value.** σ²_0 = r_0² is one observation. A large first return leaves a long tail when λ is close to 1. Some desks seed the recursion with a sample variance of an earlier window instead.
- **Look-ahead.** Using r_t² inside σ_t would mix the return you are about to score with the volatility you score it by. This recursion does not do that. Do not "fix" the index.
- **λ is not estimated here.** 0.94 is the RiskMetrics daily convention, not a maximum-likelihood estimate for your sample. The half-life of a shock is about ln(0.5)/ln(λ) periods (about 11 days at 0.94).
- **NaNs and the first call.** A NaN poisons every later value. The first call compiles; `cache=True` reuses the compiled code afterwards.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy, numba. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/numba-ewma-volatility/numba-ewma-volatility.py

```python
import numpy as np
from numba import njit

@njit(cache=True)
def ewma_vol(returns, lam=0.94):
    """EWMA volatility. var[t] uses returns[:t] only (r[t] is excluded).

    lam is the weight on the previous variance (RiskMetrics daily default 0.94).
    """
    if lam < 0.0 or lam > 1.0:
        raise ValueError("lam must be in [0, 1]")
    r = returns
    n = r.shape[0]
    var = np.empty(n, dtype=np.float64)
    if n == 0:
        return var
    var[0] = r[0] * r[0]
    one = 1.0 - lam
    for t in range(1, n):
        prev = r[t - 1]
        var[t] = lam * var[t - 1] + one * prev * prev
    return np.sqrt(var)
```

## FAQ

**Why does the variance at t use the return at t−1?**

So that the volatility sitting on row t was knowable before r_t was. That is the RiskMetrics recursion. Putting r_t into var[t] would make any later Sharpe-style scaling use information from the return it is scaling.

**Is this GARCH?**

No. GARCH(1,1) has a constant term and the two slopes are estimated. EWMA is the special case ω = 0 and α + β = 1, with λ chosen rather than fitted. It has no finite unconditional variance.

## Related

- [GARCH(1,1)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/garch/)
- [Realized Volatility](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/realized-volatility/)
- [Fast Rolling Mean, Std, Beta and Z-score with Numba](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/rolling-window-numba/)

# Resample Trade Ticks to OHLCV and VWAP Bars

> Turn a trade tape with a timestamp index into regular time bars: open, high, low, close, volume, VWAP and trade count. Empty bins are dropped.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/pandas-tick-to-ohlcv/

Category: Data Engineering for Quants. Snippet ID: `pandas-tick-to-ohlcv`.

## What it does

Time bars group irregular trades into fixed clock buckets. Open and close are the first and last trade prices in the bucket, high and low are the extrema, and volume and trade count are sums and counts. VWAP is the volume-weighted average of the trade prices inside the bucket, which is the trade-level VWAP rather than a typical-price approximation from the bar.

## Approach

```
For the trades in a clock bin of width Δ:
  open  = price of the earliest trade
  high  = max price,   low = min price
  close = price of the latest trade
  volume = Σ volume,   trades = count
  VWAP  = Σ price·volume / Σ volume     (undefined if volume is 0)

Bins with no trades are omitted.
```

## When to use it

- Building a research bar from a trade tape before a backtest or a volatility estimate.
- Checking a SQL aggregation. The same VWAP is computed in [duckdb-asof-vwap](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/duckdb-asof-vwap/) without loading the tape into pandas.
- Session VWAP across a whole day, as a benchmark rather than a bar feature, is the [VWAP](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vwap/) term.

## Pitfalls

- **Timestamp ties.** `resample` uses the index order. Two trades with the same timestamp keep whatever order the frame has, and that order decides open and close. Sort by `(timestamp, sequence)` before setting the index. The DuckDB ticks page shows the same trap.
- **Empty minutes.** They are removed, so the result is not a regular grid. Reindex against a full calendar if a model needs missing bars as gaps.
- **Zero volume.** A bucket whose volumes sum to zero gets a missing VWAP rather than a divide-by-zero. Those prints are not a price discovery event.
- **Auctions and sessions.** The resampler does not know the cash-session clock. Filter the tape to the session you mean before calling it.

## Python reference implementation

Requires pandas. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/pandas-tick-to-ohlcv/pandas-tick-to-ohlcv.py

```python
import pandas as pd

def ticks_to_bars(ticks: pd.DataFrame, freq: str = "1min") -> pd.DataFrame:
    """OHLCV, VWAP and trade count from a trade tape.

    ticks: DatetimeIndex, columns price and volume, sorted by time.
    Empty bins are dropped. VWAP is missing when the bin volume is 0.
    """
    if not isinstance(ticks.index, pd.DatetimeIndex):
        raise TypeError("ticks must be indexed by a DatetimeIndex")
    if not {"price", "volume"}.issubset(ticks.columns):
        raise ValueError("ticks need price and volume columns")
    ticks = ticks.sort_index()
    grouped = ticks.resample(freq)
    bars = grouped["price"].ohlc()
    bars["volume"] = grouped["volume"].sum()
    traded_value = (ticks["price"] * ticks["volume"]).resample(freq).sum()
    bars["vwap"] = traded_value / bars["volume"].where(bars["volume"] > 0)
    bars["trades"] = grouped["price"].count()
    return bars.dropna(subset=["open"])
```

## FAQ

**Why can VWAP differ from a typical-price bar VWAP?**

Typical price (high + low + close) / 3 times bar volume only approximates the trades. This function weights each trade by its own size, which is the VWAP used as an execution benchmark.

**What happens to a minute with no trades?**

It is omitted. The clock bin exists inside resample as an empty row and is then dropped, so you can join the result back onto a complete calendar if you need an explicit gap.

## Related

- [Volume-Weighted Average Price (VWAP)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vwap/)
- [Per-Symbol Minute VWAP in DuckDB](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/duckdb-asof-vwap/)
- [Equal-Volume Bars from a Trade Tape](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/pandas-volume-bars/)

# Equal-Volume Bars from a Trade Tape

> Group trades into bars that each contain about the same traded volume. The trade that crosses the threshold stays in the bar it completes. A single trade larger than the threshold is not split.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/pandas-volume-bars/

Category: Data Engineering for Quants. Snippet ID: `pandas-volume-bars`.

## What it does

Volume bars sample the tape by quantity instead of by clock time. Walking the trades in order, a bar closes on the trade that makes cumulative volume reach the next multiple of the threshold. Bars therefore hold roughly constant information in the sense of traded size, and the time between bars shrinks when the market is active. The last bar is returned even if it has not reached the threshold.

## Approach

```
Threshold V > 0. Trades in time order, volumes v_i ≥ 0.
Let C_i = Σ_{k≤i} v_k and C_0-side = 0 before trade i (C_{i−1}).
  bar(i) = floor( C_{i−1} / V )

The trade that pushes C_i across a multiple of V stays in the bar that was open.
A trade with v_i > V is kept whole, so that bar's volume can exceed V.
OHLC and the bar's end timestamp come from the trades in the group.
```

## Why sample by volume

- Clock bars mix quiet minutes, which are almost empty, with auction and news minutes that contain a large share of the day's volume. Volume bars put a similar amount of trading in each row.
- López de Prado argues that sampling by volume (or by information) produces return series closer to i.i.d. than sampling by the clock. That is a modelling convenience, not a source of returns by itself.
- Bars like these are the input to bucket measures such as [VPIN](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vpin/), which wants equal-volume buckets rather than equal-time buckets.

## Pitfalls

- **Do not split prints.** A block trade larger than V becomes one oversized bar. Splitting it would invent prices.
- **The closing print is included.** Floor of the cumulative volume *before* the trade is what keeps the crossing trade in the bar that fills. Floor of the cumulative volume *after* the trade pushes that trade into the next bar and leaves the earlier bar short of V.
- **Incomplete tail.** The last bar is whatever remains. Drop it before estimating a statistic that assumes every bar has volume near V.
- **Sort order is the sampling order.** A DatetimeIndex is sorted. Any other index is used as given, which is wrong if the frame is not already in exchange order.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy, pandas. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/pandas-volume-bars/pandas-volume-bars.py

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def volume_bars(ticks: pd.DataFrame, bar_volume: float) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """OHLCV bars of about `bar_volume` traded units.

    The trade that crosses each multiple of bar_volume stays in the bar it
    completes. Trades are not split. The final, possibly short, bar is kept.
    """
    if bar_volume <= 0:
        raise ValueError("bar_volume must be positive")
    if not {"price", "volume"}.issubset(ticks.columns):
        raise ValueError("ticks need price and volume columns")
    if isinstance(ticks.index, pd.DatetimeIndex):
        ticks = ticks.sort_index()
    vol = ticks["volume"].to_numpy(dtype=np.float64)
    if vol.size and np.any(vol < 0):
        raise ValueError("volume must be non-negative")
    if vol.size == 0:
        return pd.DataFrame(columns=["end_time", "open", "high", "low", "close", "volume"])
    bar_id = np.floor(np.cumsum(vol) - vol) // bar_volume
    bar_id = pd.Series(bar_id.astype(np.int64), index=ticks.index)
    grouped = ticks.groupby(bar_id, sort=True)
    out = grouped.agg(
        open=("price", "first"),
        high=("price", "max"),
        low=("price", "min"),
        close=("price", "last"),
        volume=("volume", "sum"),
    )
    out.insert(0, "end_time", grouped.tail(1).index.to_numpy())
    out.index.name = "bar_id"
    return out
```

## FAQ

**Why not use cumsum(volume) // bar_volume as the bar id?**

That assigns the trade which crosses the threshold to the next bar, so the bar you just closed is systematically short of the threshold. Using the cumulative volume before the trade keeps the crossing trade in the bar that fills.

**How should I pick the threshold?**

A common research choice is a fraction of average daily volume, so a typical day produces a similar number of bars across names. The threshold is a sampling parameter. It is not an execution instruction.

## Related

- [Resample Trade Ticks to OHLCV and VWAP Bars](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/pandas-tick-to-ohlcv/)
- [Volume-Synchronized Probability of Informed Trading (VPIN)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vpin/)
- [Realized Volatility](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/realized-volatility/)

# Rolling Hedge Ratio and Spread Z-Score

> A rolling OLS hedge ratio between two price series, the spread y − βx, and a rolling z-score of that spread. The z-score uses a second window on an already rolling spread, so it is defined later than β. Illustrative only; not a trading signal.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/pairs-zscore-signal/

Category: Time Series & Stat-Arb. Snippet ID: `pairs-zscore-signal`.

## What it does

The hedge ratio at each date is the slope of y on x over the trailing window, cov(y, x) / var(x). The spread is the residual of that slope with no intercept, y − βx. Its z-score subtracts a trailing mean and divides by a trailing sample standard deviation, both taken over the same window length. A large absolute z-score means the spread is far from its recent average. That is a description of the series, not a recommendation to trade it.

## Approach

```
β_t     = Cov_w(y, x)_t / Var_w(x)_t          (pandas sample cov and var, ddof = 1)
spread_t = y_t − β_t x_t
z_t      = (spread_t − mean_w(spread)_t) / std_w(spread)_t

β_t is defined once `window` observations exist.
z_t needs a further `window` finite spreads, so it starts about 2·window observations in.
std = 0 → z is missing, not infinite.
```

## How it sits next to cointegration

- A hedge ratio is only interesting as a mean-reverting spread if the series are [cointegrated](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/cointegration/), or at least if the spread rejects a unit root. See the [ADF](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/adf-test/) page.
- The [half-life](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/half-life-mean-reversion/) of the spread is the usual way to choose the window that standardises z, rather than picking 60 because it is round.
- The same rolling slope, compiled and re-centred, is `rolling_beta` in [rolling-window-numba](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/rolling-window-numba/).

## Pitfalls

- **No intercept.** The spread is y − βx, not y − a − βx. If the two prices differ by a level, that level sits inside the spread and the z-score spends a long time absorbing it. Engle-Granger includes an intercept.
- **Nested windows.** z_t standardises a spread that already used a window to estimate β. Early z values are noisier than a z-score of a fixed-β residual.
- **Look-ahead is not in the formulas, but it is easy to add.** β_t uses prices through t. A position decided from z_t must not trade at the close of t. Lag the position by at least one bar, as on the Polars backtest page.
- **Not a signal to trade.** A z-score of 2 is two recent standard deviations. It is not an expected return and it is not a suggestion to buy or sell the spread.

## Python reference implementation

Requires pandas. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/pairs-zscore-signal/pairs-zscore-signal.py

```python
import pandas as pd

def pair_zscore(y: pd.Series, x: pd.Series, window: int = 60) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Rolling slope of y on x, the residual spread, and its rolling z-score.

    Sample covariance and variance (ddof=1), so the ratio matches OLS with an
    intercept-free slope. Illustrative only; not a trading signal.
    """
    if window < 2:
        raise ValueError("window must be at least 2")
    y, x = y.align(x, join="inner")
    beta = y.rolling(window).cov(x) / x.rolling(window).var()
    spread = y - beta * x
    sd = spread.rolling(window).std()
    z = (spread - spread.rolling(window).mean()) / sd.where(sd > 0)
    return pd.DataFrame({"beta": beta, "spread": spread, "zscore": z})
```

## FAQ

**Why does the z-score start so late?**

The slope needs `window` rows, and the mean and standard deviation of the spread need another `window` finite spreads. With a window of 60 the z-score becomes available about 120 rows in, not 60.

**Can I trade the sign of the z-score?**

This function only standardises a spread. Whether the spread mean-reverts, whether both legs can be traded, and what it costs are separate questions. The output is not an order.

## Related

- [Cointegration (Engle-Granger & Johansen)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/cointegration/)
- [Half-Life of Mean Reversion](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/half-life-mean-reversion/)
- [Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) Test](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/adf-test/)
- [Fast Rolling Mean, Std, Beta and Z-score with Numba](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/rolling-window-numba/)

# Rolling Z-Score from a Zero-Copy Sliding Window

> Build each rolling window as a view with sliding_window_view and reduce it in NumPy. The view shares memory with the input. Sample standard deviation of zero becomes a missing z-score, not an infinity.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/numpy-strided-rolling/

Category: High-Performance Python. Snippet ID: `numpy-strided-rolling`.

## What it does

sliding_window_view reshapes a 1-D array into overlapping windows of length w without copying the values. The row means and sample standard deviations are then ordinary NumPy reductions along the window axis. The z-score at the right edge of each window is (x − mean) / std. Positions before the first full window are missing. This is a convenient form when the reduction is a NumPy ufunc. It is not always faster than a single running-sum pass, because each overlapping row still reads w elements.

## Approach

```
W = sliding_window_view(x, w)          shape (n − w + 1, w), a view
μ = mean(W, axis=1)                    population mean of the window
s = std(W, axis=1, ddof=1)             sample standard deviation
z_{w−1+i} = (x_{w−1+i} − μ_i) / s_i     if s_i > 0, else missing

Memory: W.base is x. Changing W would change x.
```

## When to use it

- A one-off rolling reduction that NumPy already implements (mean, quantile, median), where writing a running-sum update is not worth it.
- Teaching or testing a window statistic against an obvious definition. The view makes the window explicit.
- For mean, variance and beta on long series, a running sum does one pass and less memory traffic. See [rolling-window-numba](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/rolling-window-numba/) and [cython-rolling-mean](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/cython-rolling-mean/).

## Pitfalls

- **It is a view.** Do not write into the window array. The write lands in the original series.
- **The view is O(n·w) to reduce** even though it is O(1) extra memory to build. A rolling mean this way is slower than a prefix sum for large w.
- **ddof.** Sample standard deviation (divide by w−1) matches pandas `rolling.std`. Population standard deviation does not. w must be at least 2.
- **Zero variation.** A window of identical values has sample std 0. Division is skipped and the z-score is missing.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/numpy-strided-rolling/numpy-strided-rolling.py

```python
import numpy as np
from numpy.lib.stride_tricks import sliding_window_view

def rolling_zscore(x, window: int) -> np.ndarray:
    """Rolling z-score using a zero-copy sliding window.

    Sample standard deviation (ddof=1). Warm-up and zero-std windows are NaN.
    The window view is not writable from the caller's point of view: this
    function only reads it.
    """
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=np.float64).reshape(-1)
    window = int(window)
    if window < 2:
        raise ValueError("window must be at least 2")
    out = np.full(x.shape, np.nan)
    if x.size < window:
        return out
    view = sliding_window_view(x, window)
    mu = view.mean(axis=1)
    sd = view.std(axis=1, ddof=1)
    z = np.full(mu.shape, np.nan)
    np.divide(x[window - 1:] - mu, sd, out=z, where=sd > 0)
    out[window - 1:] = z
    return out
```

## FAQ

**Does sliding_window_view copy the data?**

No. It returns a view with modified strides. The extra memory is a small array header, not n times w floats. The subsequent mean and std do read each window, so the compute is not free.

**Why not use this for every rolling statistic?**

Reductions that have an O(1) update, such as a sum, are faster and kinder to the cache as a single pass. The strided view is the right tool when the statistic is awkward to update, for example a rolling median or quantile.

## Related

- [Fast Rolling Mean, Std, Beta and Z-score with Numba](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/rolling-window-numba/)
- [O(n) Rolling Mean (Cython Memoryview Recurrence)](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/cython-rolling-mean/)

# Top-of-Book Queue Imbalance while Replaying Quotes

> Walk a tape of best-bid and best-ask sizes in a compiled loop and emit the queue imbalance at each update. A locked or empty touch, where the two sizes sum to zero, is recorded as zero rather than as a division by zero.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/numba-order-book-replay/

Category: High-Performance Python. Snippet ID: `numba-order-book-replay`.

## What it does

Queue imbalance at the touch is the bid size minus the ask size, divided by the sum of the two. It is positive when more size is displayed on the bid than on the ask. Replaying the top-of-book tape means evaluating that ratio at every update, in order, without building an intermediate DataFrame. The function does not reconstruct price levels and it does not infer trade direction. It is the size ratio only.

## Approach

```
I_t = (q^b_t − q^a_t) / (q^b_t + q^a_t)    if q^b_t + q^a_t > 0
    = 0                                         otherwise

−1 ≤ I_t ≤ 1
I_t = 1  → all displayed touch size is on the bid
I_t = −1 → all of it is on the ask
Sizes must be ≥ 0. This is not Cont–Kukanov–Stoikov order-flow imbalance.
```

## Where it fits

- A feature on a quote tape: one number per book update, cheap enough to compute inside a compiled replay of millions of rows.
- As a simpler cousin of [order-flow imbalance](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/ofi/). OFI uses price changes and the size that was added or removed. Queue imbalance uses only the sizes currently displayed.
- Trade-sign toxicity measures such as [VPIN](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vpin/) need trades, not this quote ratio.

## Pitfalls

- **Displayed size is not the true queue.** Iceberg orders, hidden liquidity and fleeting quotes mean the ratio is a picture of what was shown, not of demand.
- **Crossed or zero sizes.** A feed glitch can report a zero or negative size. Negative sizes raise. A zero total returns 0 so one bad print does not poison a later reduction with NaN, but you should still count how often that branch hits.
- **Not comparable across names without care.** The ratio is already scale-free. Its variance still depends on how often the touch flips, which differs between a thick future and a thin stock.

## Python reference implementation

Requires numpy, numba. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/numba-order-book-replay/numba-order-book-replay.py

```python
import numpy as np
from numba import njit

@njit(cache=True)
def queue_imbalance(bid_sz, ask_sz):
    """Queue imbalance (bid_sz - ask_sz) / (bid_sz + ask_sz) at each update.

    Replay order is the array order. Total size of 0 yields 0. Negative sizes raise.
    """
    n = bid_sz.shape[0]
    if ask_sz.shape[0] != n:
        raise ValueError("bid_sz and ask_sz must have the same length")
    out = np.empty(n, dtype=np.float64)
    for i in range(n):
        b = bid_sz[i]
        a = ask_sz[i]
        if b < 0.0 or a < 0.0:
            raise ValueError("sizes must be non-negative")
        tot = b + a
        out[i] = (b - a) / tot if tot > 0.0 else 0.0
    return out
```

## FAQ

**How is this different from order-flow imbalance?**

Order-flow imbalance adds up changes at the best quotes: size added on the bid is buying pressure, size added on the ask is selling pressure. Queue imbalance ignores the change and only looks at the sizes currently sitting at the touch.

**Why return 0 when both sizes are 0?**

There is no queue to compare. Returning NaN is also defensible; 0 keeps a compiled reduction from turning the rest of a session into NaN when a single empty update appears. Check the rate of empty updates separately.

## Related

- [Order Flow Imbalance (OFI)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/ofi/)
- [Volume-Synchronized Probability of Informed Trading (VPIN)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vpin/)

# Attach the Prevailing Quote to Each Trade

> Backward as-of join, per symbol, from trades to the latest quote at or before the trade. Trade side is then +1 above the mid, −1 below it, 0 at the mid, and missing when no quote has printed yet.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/polars-asof-join-quotes/

Category: Data Engineering for Quants. Snippet ID: `polars-asof-join-quotes`.

## What it does

An as-of join matches each trade to the most recent quote that was already on the book, rather than to a quote with the same timestamp only. Doing it by symbol keeps one name's quote from attaching to another name's trade. The side rule compares the trade price to the matched mid-price. It is a labelling convention for research, not the exchange's aggressor flag.

## Approach

```
For each trade (symbol s, time t), choose the quote of s with the greatest t_q ≤ t.
  mid = (bid + ask) / 2
  side =  1  if price > mid
       = −1  if price < mid
       =  0  if price = mid
       = missing if no quote has t_q ≤ t

Both frames are sorted by time before the join. Exact timestamp matches are allowed.
```

## Why backward, and by symbol

- A trade can only be labelled with a quote the matching engine had already published. A forward as-of join would use a future quote. That is look-ahead.
- `by="symbol"` is the difference between a usable tape and a join that pastes the wrong book onto a print whenever two names trade at close times.
- The labelled tape is an input to signed-volume measures such as [Kyle's lambda](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/kyles-lambda/) and to the buy and sell buckets in [VPIN](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vpin/).

## Pitfalls

- **No tolerance by default.** The latest quote might be hours old, or from the previous session. Pass a tolerance if a stale quote should not label a trade.
- **Quote rule is not Lee-Ready.** The full tick test also looks at whether the quote itself moved. A price above the mid is only a clue about the aggressor.
- **Sort both sides.** `join_asof` requires the time key to be sorted. This function sorts by time. A secondary sequence number should already have broken ties in the frame you pass in, or two events in the same timestamp keep their original relative order only if the sort is stable, which Polars' default sort is.
- **Missing quote is not side 0.** Side 0 means the trade printed at the mid. A trade before the first quote has a missing side. Collapsing both to 0 hides a join failure.

## Python reference implementation

Requires polars. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/polars-asof-join-quotes/polars-asof-join-quotes.py

```python
import polars as pl

def tag_trades_with_quotes(trades: pl.DataFrame, quotes: pl.DataFrame, tolerance=None) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Backward as-of join of quotes onto trades, per symbol, plus a mid rule.

    side is +1 above the mid, -1 below, 0 at the mid, and null if no quote
    is available at or before the trade. tolerance drops quotes older than that.
    """
    need_t = {"symbol", "ts", "price"}
    need_q = {"symbol", "ts", "bid", "ask"}
    if not need_t.issubset(trades.columns) or not need_q.issubset(quotes.columns):
        raise ValueError("trades need symbol, ts, price; quotes need symbol, ts, bid, ask")
    out = (
        trades.sort("ts")
        .join_asof(
            quotes.sort("ts"),
            on="ts",
            by="symbol",
            strategy="backward",
            tolerance=tolerance,
            check_sortedness=False,
        )
    )
    mid = (pl.col("bid") + pl.col("ask")) / 2
    known = mid.is_not_null()
    return out.with_columns(
        side=pl.when(known & (pl.col("price") > mid)).then(pl.lit(1))
        .when(known & (pl.col("price") < mid)).then(pl.lit(-1))
        .when(known).then(pl.lit(0))
        .otherwise(pl.lit(None))
    )
```

## FAQ

**Why not join on an equal timestamp?**

Quotes and trades rarely share a timestamp. An inner join on ts drops almost every trade. An as-of join keeps the quote that was current, which is the one a labelling rule can actually use.

**What does a missing side mean?**

No quote for that symbol had a timestamp at or before the trade, or the matched quote was older than the tolerance. It does not mean the trade was at the mid. At-mid trades have side 0.

## Related

- [Kyle's Lambda](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/kyles-lambda/)
- [Volume-Synchronized Probability of Informed Trading (VPIN)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vpin/)
- [Order Flow Imbalance (OFI)](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/ofi/)

# Per-Symbol Minute VWAP in DuckDB

> Aggregate a Parquet trade tape to one VWAP and one volume per symbol per minute, in a single DuckDB query. The file path is a bound parameter. Despite the page slug, this is a time-bucket aggregation, not an as-of join.
> URL: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/duckdb-asof-vwap/

Category: Data Engineering for Quants. Snippet ID: `duckdb-asof-vwap`.

## What it does

Minute VWAP is the traded value in that minute divided by the traded volume, computed separately for each symbol. DuckDB's time_bucket assigns each timestamp to the start of its minute, and GROUP BY ALL groups by the selected symbol and minute columns. Division uses NULLIF so a minute whose volume sums to zero gets a missing VWAP instead of an error or an infinity. The path to the Parquet files is passed as a parameter.

## Approach

```
minute = time_bucket(INTERVAL 1 MINUTE, timestamp)
VWAP   = Σ(price · volume) / Σ volume     within (symbol, minute)
volume = Σ volume

SELECT symbol, minute, VWAP, volume
FROM read_parquet(?)          -- path is bound, not concatenated
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY symbol, minute
```

## When to use it

- You want minute bars from a large tape and you do not want to materialise every tick as a DataFrame. The aggregation runs in DuckDB and only the bars come back.
- The same VWAP, computed after loading the ticks, is [pandas-tick-to-ohlcv](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/pandas-tick-to-ohlcv/). Session VWAP as an execution benchmark is the [VWAP](https://quantcore-labs.com/glossary/vwap/) term.
- Attaching quotes to trades is a different operation. That as-of join is [polars-asof-join-quotes](https://quantcore-labs.com/code/polars-asof-join-quotes/). This query does not look at quotes.

## Pitfalls

- **The slug says asof.** The query is a group-by on a time bucket. There is no ASOF JOIN in it. Keeping the slug stable matters more than renaming the page to match the SQL keyword.
- **Timestamp ties and order.** VWAP does not care which trade came first. Open and close would. Do not extend this query with an unordered `first(price)` and call it the open.
- **Zero volume.** `NULLIF` makes VWAP null when the minute's volume is 0. The row is still returned, so a caller can see the empty minute. Filter it if you want only real bars.
- **Clock and time zone.** `time_bucket` uses the timestamp as stored. Naive and timezone-aware columns must not be mixed across files.

## Python reference implementation

Requires duckdb. Tested before publication and re-executed with assertions on every rebuild. MIT licensed. Raw file: https://quantcore-labs.com/code/duckdb-asof-vwap/duckdb-asof-vwap.py

```python
import duckdb

def minute_vwap(parquet_glob: str):
    """Minute VWAP and volume per symbol from Parquet trades.

    parquet_glob is a bound parameter (a file path or a glob). The query is an
    aggregation on time_bucket, not an as-of join.
    """
    if not isinstance(parquet_glob, str) or parquet_glob == "":
        raise ValueError("parquet_glob must be a non-empty string")
    con = duckdb.connect()
    return con.execute(
        """
        SELECT symbol,
               time_bucket(INTERVAL 1 MINUTE, timestamp) AS minute,
               SUM(price * volume) / NULLIF(SUM(volume), 0) AS vwap,
               SUM(volume) AS volume
        FROM read_parquet(?)
        GROUP BY ALL
        ORDER BY symbol, minute
        """,
        [parquet_glob],
    ).df()
```

## FAQ

**Why is this not an as-of join?**

VWAP needs every trade in the minute, weighted by size. An as-of join would keep a single neighbouring row. The page id was fixed by the batch that added it; the SQL matches the definition above, and the as-of join lives on the Polars quotes page.

**Why bind the path?**

The glob is data. Concatenating it into the query string turns a peculiar folder name into SQL syntax. read_parquet(?) keeps it a parameter, including globs.
